A decade ago, the coastal town of Marren's Point depended almost entirely on the summer fishing season. Today its harbour is lined with cafes, the old cannery houses a small museum, and the population has nearly doubled. The transformation did not happen by accident. It followed a bitter planning dispute that divided neighbours and eventually reached the state's highest court.

The dispute began when a developer proposed converting the abandoned fish-processing plant into a hotel and conference centre. Supporters argued that the project would bring year-round employment, while opponents warned that it would price local families out of the housing market. Public meetings grew so heated that the town council hired an outside mediator.

According to the minutes of the first session, the mediator opened by asking both sides to describe, without interruption, what they feared most. The developer's representative said the plant would collapse if nothing were done. Residents said the character of the town would be lost. Neither side changed its position that evening, but the tone of the debate shifted.

Over the following months the council commissioned an independent economic assessment. The report, produced by a consultancy based two hours inland, concluded that a smaller development restricted to the cannery itself would create more local jobs per dollar invested than the original proposal. It also recommended a community land trust to keep a share of new housing affordable in perpetuity.

The council adopted most of the recommendations. The developer scaled back the plan, the trust was established with an initial endowment, and construction began the next spring. Not everyone was satisfied. The owner of the largest remaining fishing boat, who had campaigned against the project from the start, told the council that the town had traded its working waterfront for a postcard.

The episode is now taught in a graduate course on land-use planning. Students read the mediation minutes, the economic report and the court judgment together, and they are asked to identify the moment when compromise became possible. Most pick the first session, when each side was forced to listen. A few argue that nothing changed until the money was on the table.

In an interview with the campus radio station last spring, the mediator was asked what she remembered most. She said she recalled the silence after the residents finished speaking, and how long it took before anyone was willing to break it. The final report, she added, confirmed to the council that careful listening can change a negotiation more than any argument. She has advised a dozen other towns since then, and she tells the same story every time.

Visitors now travel to Marren's Point to see the result for themselves. The cannery houses a cooperative bakery on the ground floor and affordable flats above. The fishing boats still leave before dawn, though there are fewer of them, and the cafes open in time to serve the crews when they return.

The town library received the Whitcombe collection on a damp Tuesday in March, when two removal vans backed into the loading yard behind the reading room. The bequest had been assembled over five decades by a local surveyor who kept every receipt, every map, and every letter, and the staff had been told to expect roughly forty boxes of mixed material. What arrived was closer to ninety: crates of ledgers, biscuit tins packed with photographs, rolls of estate plans tied with garden twine, and a filing cabinet whose drawers had swollen shut with damp.

The first task was triage. Volunteers carried each crate into the conservation room and recorded its condition on a clipboard, noting mould, water staining, insect damage, and the occasional nest built by mice. The paper in the lower boxes had buckled after a leak in the storage unit, and the ink on some of the estate plans had begun to migrate into the fibres, producing the soft blue halo that paper conservators call feathering. The photographs were worse: many had stuck together in blocks, and separating them required slow humidification over several days.

Storage was another problem. The reading room had no spare shelving, so the crates sat in a corridor for a fortnight while the staff ordered archival boxes and waited for a delivery of acid-free folders. In the meantime the volunteers worked at two trestle tables, wearing gloves and aprons, sorting envelopes into piles by decade. The oldest material dated from the 1840s, the newest from the 1970s, and the gaps between the piles were as informative as the contents: whole years of correspondence had been lost to a fire in the 1930s, and the surveyor left those gaps unfilled.

The collection arrived uncatalogued, and the surveyor's own ordering, if it could be called an ordering, mixed family correspondence with drainage surveys and shopping lists. A pair of volunteers began reconstructing the original sequence from dates pencilled on the backs of envelopes, while a third sorted the maps by parish. The work was slow, and the reading room closed early for most of the spring.

By June the staff had emptied thirty boxes, treated the worst of the water damage, and begun a rough inventory. The collection included several hundred letters, a run of parish rate books, and a set of field notebooks, several of which were water-damaged and required conservation before cataloguing. The notebooks turned out to be the most valuable part of the bequest, since they recorded hedgerows and footpaths that no longer appear on modern maps.

The library now plans a small exhibition in the autumn, with the notebooks at its centre and a reading list for visitors who want to trace the footpaths themselves.

The Riverton water treatment plant draws from the Mill Creek reservoir and serves about 84,000 households across the northern half of the county. Built in 1974 and expanded twice since, the plant can process up to 60 million litres a day, though average demand is closer to 38 million. Raw water enters through a pair of intake screens that keep out leaves, fish and debris larger than a few millimetres, and is then dosed with alum so that suspended clay and organic matter clump together and settle out.

From the settling basins the water passes through eight rapid gravity filters, each filled with a metre of anthracite over a bed of sand. Operators backwash the filters every 40 to 60 hours, depending on turbidity, using treated water stored in a raised tank beside the filter hall. After filtration the water is disinfected with chlorine and, since 2016, with ultraviolet light as a second barrier against Cryptosporidium and other chlorine-tolerant organisms. Fluoride is added for dental health and lime to raise the pH so that the water does not corrode the lead service lines still found in some of the older neighbourhoods.

The plant laboratory tests samples at every stage, from the reservoir intake to the finished water leaving the site, and the results are published in the annual water quality report each spring. Residents who want to know what is in their water can search that report by postcode; the utility also posts notices when a flushing programme or a main repair is likely to discolour supplies in a particular street. Questions about a specific address go to the customer service line, which is staffed on weekdays.

The upgrade now under construction will replace the oldest filter gallery and add a second ultraviolet reactor, work that the county says will take about 18 months and will be paid for out of existing reserves rather than a rate increase. During the work the plant will run at reduced capacity, and the utility may ask some large industrial customers to shift their heaviest demand to overnight hours. Households on the higher ground north of the river receive water from a separate booster station, which maintains pressure through the summer months when demand roughly doubles.

The Wexford Estate is a historic country house and landscaped garden complex in the upper valley, first recorded in the sixteenth century as a fortified manor held by a family of wool merchants. The original hall was rebuilt twice, once after a fire in 1712 and again in the 1790s, when the west wing was extended and the terraced gardens were laid out in the fashionable manner of the period. The gardens were designed by a landscape architect who had worked on several comparable estates and who is known chiefly through a surviving plan and a bundle of letters now held in the local archive.

Visitors approaching from the south pass through a beech avenue planted in 1804 and then cross a stone bridge over the mill stream that once powered a small grain mill. The mill ceased operation early in the twentieth century and its machinery was sold at auction in 1911; only the wheel pit and part of the sluice remain. Beyond the bridge the drive curves between lawns and specimen trees, including several cedars and a Lebanon cedar said to have been raised from seed brought back from a tour of the Levant.

The main house is built of local limestone with slate roofs and is arranged around a small courtyard. Its interior retains much of its eighteenth-century character: a flagged entrance hall, a cantilevered staircase, and a series of drawing rooms with original plasterwork. The library was enlarged in 1830 to house a collection of several thousand volumes, most of which were dispersed at a sale in the 1950s, although the pressed-tin ceiling and the mahogany shelving survive intact.

The estate passed through several branches of the family before being sold in 1907 to a shipping magnate, who modernised the house with central heating and electric light and who commissioned a new range of glasshouses. During the middle decades of the twentieth century the house was used first as a convalescent home and later as a school, and a number of internal partitions were introduced at that time. A restoration programme begun in the 1970s removed many of these additions and returned the principal rooms to their earlier proportions.

The grounds today comprise formal gardens, a walled kitchen garden, an arboretum, and about forty hectares of parkland grazed by a small flock of sheep. The walled garden is planted with vegetables, cutting flowers and espaliered fruit trees, and the glasshouses have been restored to working order. A cafe occupies the old stable block, and an exhibition in the former dairy explains the history of the estate.

The estate is administered by a charitable trust that also manages two neighbouring properties. Enquiries about group visits, filming, and the loan of objects from the collection should be sent in writing to the estate office at 118 Chestnut Street in the town of Springfield, ZIP code 62704, and not to the house itself, which receives no postal delivery. A small museum shop beside the ticket office sells guidebooks, postcards and reproductions of the eighteenth-century garden plan.

Certificate rotation on the internal mail relay has confused several teams this quarter, so these notes collect what we learned during the migration in March. The relay runs on the small cluster in the east data centre, and it terminates TLS for both the submission and the IMAP endpoints. Historically the certificate was installed by hand once a year, which worked fine when there were two hosts and a single administrator. That arrangement stopped being practical after the cluster grew to eleven nodes, each with its own key, and after the security team began demanding that keys never leave the host that generated them. The first attempt at automation used a shared NFS export for the key material, but the export was readable by every node, so the team abandoned it after a week. The second attempt used a small internal service that held the keys in memory and served them over mTLS; that worked, but the service itself became a single point of failure and had to be restarted during a maintenance window that nobody had documented. What finally worked was simpler than either of the earlier approaches. Each node generates its own key locally and keeps it in the secure store that ships with the operating system. A timer runs twice a day and asks the internal ACME endpoint for a certificate, presenting a token that the load balancer validates before it forwards the request. The endpoint signs the request and returns the chain, and the timer writes both the certificate and the chain into the directory the relay already reads. Reloading the relay is the only step that touches the running process, and it happens without dropping connections because the new certificate is picked up on the next handshake rather than at startup. Monitoring caused more trouble than the certificates themselves. The old checks looked at the expiry date of a single file, which told us nothing once there were eleven files on eleven hosts. The replacement check asks each node for the fingerprint it is currently serving and compares it with the fingerprint the endpoint issued most recently. A mismatch raises a warning rather than a page, because a short window of mismatch is normal while a reload is in flight, and paging on it produced a week of noise before anyone thought to widen the tolerance. The fingerprint check also caught a case where a node had been restored from a snapshot and was serving a key that no longer existed anywhere else. To replace the certificate on a single node by hand, open the admin console, go to Settings / Security / Certificates, and choose the node from the list on the left. The page shows the fingerprint currently in use and a button that requests a fresh one from the endpoint. Press it, wait for the status line to turn green, and reload the relay from the same page. If the status line stays amber, the token was rejected and the node clock is probably wrong. Most of the remaining questions were about the old hosts, which are being retired in the autumn, and about whether the timer should run more often during a migration window.

A while back I wrote in about the sync problem on the archive server and promised to report what happened, so here it is. The short version is that nothing was broken and the whole thing was a misunderstanding on my part, but the long version is more interesting and might save someone else the afternoon I lost. It started when the nightly job began failing with a permission error on a directory that I was sure existed. I asked in the channel how to check whether the directory was really there, and someone suggested I look at the mount table. I ran the mount command and stared at the output for a while without understanding much of it. The mount table listed a share under /mnt/archive that I did not recognise, pointing at a hostname that looked wrong. I assumed at first that someone had changed the configuration overnight, and I spent an hour reading the change log, which turned out to be empty. Then I wondered whether the machine had rebooted into the wrong profile, and I checked the uptime, which was four hundred days. The answer, when it came, was embarrassing. The archive share had been moved to the new storage box in February, and the old hostname had been kept as an alias for exactly this kind of lag. The alias had expired, quietly, at the end of the quarter. My job was still writing to the old name, and the error was not a permission problem at all but a name that no longer resolved. The permission message was a red herring produced by the wrapper script, which reported the first non-zero exit it saw regardless of which command produced it. I found this out by accident while reading the wrapper for an unrelated reason. I had gone looking for the retry logic and instead found the error handling, which was three lines long and caught everything. The person who wrote it had left a comment saying that this was good enough for now. So the fix, in the end, was a one-line change to the configuration, and the job has been running ever since. I am told the wrapper has since been rewritten by someone who knows what they are doing, and that the error messages are now specific enough to be useful. I have not looked at it myself. I would rather not jinx it.

The harbour at Port Esk lies at the end of a single-track road, and for most of the year the only traffic is the fish lorry that comes down before dawn. In January the light arrives late and leaves early, and the water in the basin sits flat and black under a sky the colour of wet slate. The pier was built in 1887 from blocks of local granite, and the iron rings set into it have been worn smooth by a century of mooring ropes. Fishing is a small trade now: four boats work the grounds outside the bay, and the catch is landed, iced and driven south the same morning.

In 1989 the light in the lighthouse above the breakwater was automated, and the keeper's cottage beside it has stood empty since then. Salt has got into the mortar, and a strip of render has come away along the north wall. Nobody has been able to say what should be done about the roof, and the estimate from the building firm in the county town was thought too high for a structure that no longer houses anyone. In summer the cottage is used for storage; in winter the door is locked and the shutters are closed.

The tide runs hard across the mouth of the bay, and the channel shifts after every winter storm. Local charts are corrected by hand each spring, and the buoys are lifted, repainted and relaid in a sequence that has not changed in forty years. The old lifeboat station on the western side was decommissioned in 1974 and is now a store for nets and floats; a notice on the door gives a telephone number for the harbour office and a line about the byelaws.

Weather comes in from the south-west for most of the year, and the worst of it arrives without much warning. The barometer in the office is read twice a day, and the readings go into a ledger that is kept in a cupboard by the window. The ledger goes back to 1953, and the handwriting changes four or five times across the volumes, but the columns are the same: date, time, pressure, wind, visibility, remarks. A gap of eleven weeks in the winter of 1963 has never been explained, and the page where it falls has been folded over so many times that the paper has split along the crease.

The boatyard behind the quay is worked by two men and a dog, and the shed is full of half-finished hulls that have not moved in a decade. A sign above the door advertises repairs, but the telephone number painted on it was disconnected years ago. The slipway still works, and a boat can be hauled out on a spring tide if the booking is made early enough in the year.

The northern expedition spent its third winter trapped beyond the ice shelf, and morale among the crew sank lower with every week of darkness. Captain Ellery ordered the coal rationed to a handful each evening, while the surgeon inventoried bandages, tonics, and dried herbs in the freezing dispensary. In February a scouting party crossed the pressure ridges toward the basalt cliffs, dragging a sledge loaded with pemmican, kerosene, and brass surveying instruments. They mapped inlets, measured glacier drift, and carved cairns from loose shale along the headlands. One thaw brought meltwater flooding through the lower deck, ruining sacks of flour and swelling the timber bulkheads. The carpenter rebuilt bunks from salvaged pine, and the cook stretched seal meat with barley for another fortnight. Gulls returned in March, wheeling over open leads where narwhals surfaced among grinding floes. The wireless operator tapped nightly signals through static, hoping for a reply from the relief steamer. Spring storms battered the rigging, snapping lines and burying the deck in sleet. By June the ice began to groan and shift, opening a narrow channel toward the open sea. Lookouts spotted seals basking on pans, and hunters restocked the larder with fresh meat. The naturalist catalogued mosses, lichens, and fossil shells gathered from the thawed moraine. Charts were redrawn, compasses recalibrated, and chronometers checked against noon sights. When the relief ship finally appeared through the mist, flags were raised and every whistle sounded at once. The crew ferried crates of specimens, journals, and photographic plates across the heaving gangway. Ellery signed the manifest, thanked the rescuers, and ordered the anchor weighed. The exhausted vessel turned southward into rolling swells as seabirds trailed in its wake. The crew logged the position and extinguished the lamps.

The survey began in the spring of 1908, when a small party of botanists was sent north to map the flora of one highland valley and, a month later, of the neighbouring one. The two valleys lie within a single parish, yet a ridge of granite runs along the whole length of the divide, and the passes stay snowbound until late June. Nothing in the earlier literature suggested that the two plant communities would turn out to be interesting.

The party worked slowly. Most mornings they rose before dawn, walked the transects marked out the previous evening, and pressed every specimen they could identify into a field press. A hand lens and a pocket barometer were the only instruments they carried; the rest of the equipment stayed at the bothy, lashed down under a tarpaulin. Rain interrupted the work on eleven days out of twenty, and on three occasions the party was forced back to the valley floor before noon.

The northern valley is narrow, steep-sided, and shaded for much of the day. Its thin soil drains quickly, and the exposed rock carries a pale crust of lichen that the botanists had not seen anywhere else in the county. The southern valley, by contrast, opens out into a broad bowl of damp meadow, and the streams there run clear over gravel rather than cutting through peat. The botanists expected richer grassland and perhaps a few species that the northern site lacked, but they found the same sedges, the same mosses, and the same stubborn mat of heather wherever they looked.

The party's guide was a shepherd named Aonghas, who had lived on the ridge since boyhood and who insisted that the two valleys had once been joined by a shallow col, long since eroded. He could name every burn and every crag, and he refused to cross the ridge after dark, whatever the season. His account of the old tracks was recorded in the notebook, though nobody thought to check it.

The weather worsened in August. Two bridges were carried away in a single night, and the party lost a week waiting for the water to fall. Provisions ran low, and the last fortnight was spent on oatmeal, dried fish, and tea boiled in a blackened kettle.

The bothy itself was a single room of dry stone, roofed in slate and heated by a cast-iron stove that smoked whenever the wind came round to the west. The party slept on straw pallets and took turns to fetch water.

When the lists were finally laid side by side in the autumn, the species recorded in the northern valley were almost indistinguishable from those recorded in the southern one, although the soils, the drainage, and the exposure all seemed very different. The report was filed without comment, and the survey was not repeated.

The Apollo program was the third human spaceflight programme undertaken by NASA, using the Saturn IB and Saturn V launch vehicles. It began after the announcement in 1961 that the United States would attempt to land a crew before the decade was out. Each mission carried three astronauts, two of whom descended to the surface in the lunar module while the third remained in orbit. The crews collected rock samples, deployed experiments, and drove a battery-powered rover across the regolith. News of the first landing on the Moon was watched by an estimated six hundred million people, and the pictures sent back were reproduced on front pages around the world. The programme was not without risk: a fire during a ground test killed three astronauts in 1967, and an explosion on the way out nearly ended another flight in 1970. Engineers redesigned the spacecraft and rewrote procedures in response. Later missions brought back more material and stayed longer. When the last flight returned in December 1972, the samples filled a laboratory in Houston, and analysis of them continued for decades. Much of what geologists now believe about its early history comes from those few hundred kilograms of rock. The programme also produced the photographs and film that shaped how a generation imagined spaceflight.

Dozens of trawlers still tie up along the north quay before dawn, and by six the auction hall is loud with crates of haddock, mackerel and langoustine. For most of the twentieth century the boats were family-owned; skippers passed their licences to sons and daughters, and vessels rarely changed hands outside the town. In the 1990s quotas and fuel prices forced many families to sell, and a handful of processing companies bought up the older hulls. The harbor authority now lists forty-one registered fishing vessels, though only twenty-six sailed last season. The rest are laid up along the west wall, their engines stripped, their decks slowly filling with rain. The town council has debated a heritage scheme that would turn two of the oldest hulls into floating museums, but the funding has not materialised. The ice plant, rebuilt after the storm of 2011, runs at half capacity, and the fish market has cut its opening hours twice. Younger crews have drifted to Aberdeen and Peterhead, and the school on the hill has lost a third of its pupils. Even so, the season's landings have held steady, and the co-operative that runs the auction has reported a small surplus. Visitors often remark on how quiet the place feels compared with the postcard harbors further up the coast. There are no tour boats, no seafood restaurants on the pier, and the old smokehouse has been closed since the health inspection. What remains is a working waterfront: fuel trucks, ice, rope, and the low diesel hum that starts before first light. The fishermen who still sail say the margins are thinner every year, that the price paid at the auction has barely moved in a decade while the cost of gear has doubled. Several have taken second jobs in the winter, driving lorries or working on the wind farms offshore. The co-operative has tried to market a premium label for line-caught fish, and the first trial shipment has already gone to restaurants in Edinburgh and London. The Ardent Star, a sixty-foot trawler that has worked these waters since 1987, is one of the few boats that still lands a full catch every week. Its skipper, Mairi Sinclair, a third-generation fisherman, has argued for years that the small fleet is worth preserving. She has twice addressed the Scottish Parliament on quota reform, and the co-operative has printed her pamphlet for every member.

Cast-iron stoves repay a little seasonal maintenance with decades of service. Begin by lifting the lid from the flue collar and brushing soot from the baffle with a stiff wire brush. Inspect the firebox for cracks; a hairline fracture wider than 0.5 mm should be sealed with furnace cement before the first frost. Remove the ash pan, empty the grate, and scrape carbon deposits from the brick liner. The door hinge pin may seize after long exposure to heat, so apply a drop of graphite oil to the pivot and work the latch until it swings freely. Check the gasket around the loading door: a flattened rope seal leaks air and lets the fire burn too hot. Replace the gasket, press it into the channel with a putty knife, and close the door on a sheet of paper to confirm an even grip.

Before lighting the first fire of autumn, test the draft with a smouldering twist of newspaper held near the open damper; the flame should bend toward the firebox. If smoke spills into the room, inspect the chimney for a bird's nest, a collapsed liner or a plug of soot. The chimney cap should sit at least 60 cm above the ridge of the roof and 3 m from any nearby tree, or downdrafts will push smoke back through the damper. During the burning season, sweep the pipe every six weeks and watch for creosote glazing along the upper sections. A magnetic thermometer clipped to the stovepipe helps keep the flue gas between 150 and 400 degrees Celsius; cooler exhaust condenses tar, while hotter exhaust wastes fuel and can warp the baffle.

When the stove is cold, oil the damper rod, tighten the bolts on the legs, and touch up scratches with stove black. Store a bucket of dry sand beside the hearth for emergencies, and keep the brush, poker and shovel hanging on their hooks. At the end of winter, empty the ash bin, wipe the enamel with a damp cloth, and leave the air intake open a finger's width so moisture can escape. A thin film of rust on the top plate can be scrubbed away with steel wool and a little linseed oil, then buffed with a soft rag. Keep a spare firebrick on hand, since the rear brick shields the steel shell from the hottest part of the coal bed and a cracked brick should be swapped before the next heating season. Wipe the glass with a paste of wood ash and water, rinse it with clear water, and dry it with a lint-free cloth, because commercial cleaners can etch the ceramic over time. Never vacuum warm ash, since a live ember can smoulder inside the bag for hours. Finally, record the date of each sweeping on a card taped inside the door so the service history travels with the stove.

The harbour register was kept in a room above the chandlery, and Elias Vane had written every entry in it for thirty years. He sharpened his pencil each morning with a small brass knife, licked the tip, and began with the date in the top left corner. The fishermen called him the bookkeeper of the tide, though he had never learned to swim and grew uneasy whenever the wind came off the water.

The summer the pier was condemned, a surveyor came down from the city with a satchel of instruments. He measured the stonework, tapped the pilings with a hammer, and produced a report full of figures that nobody in the village could interpret. At the meeting in the church hall he explained that the outer arm had shifted by nine inches and would have to be rebuilt from the foundations. The fishermen asked what that would cost. The surveyor gave them a number, and the room went quiet.

Elias listened from the back, near the door, in the coat he wore in all weathers. He had no stake in the pier. His salary came from a fund set up a century earlier, when the port still handled timber and coal, and nobody had ever proposed to spend that money on repairs. Still, he took notes in his own notebook, in the same careful hand he used for the register.

The work began in April and ran for two seasons. Scaffolding covered the outer arm like a cage, and cranes leaned over the water in the evenings with their lamps swinging. Elias watched from the window above the chandlery. When the crews knocked off at six, the men walked into the village to drink and argue about football, and the stones were left to the gulls.

On the day the new section was unveiled, a photographer came from the newspaper and asked the harbourmaster to stand at the corner of the rebuilt arm. The harbourmaster refused. He said the job was nothing to be proud of, since the money might have gone to the lifeboat. The photographer photographed the gulls instead and printed them above a caption about progress.

Elias held his own small ceremony at dusk. He carried the ledger down to the water, opened it at a fresh page, and wrote the date. Then, because the page looked bare, he wrote one line in the remarks column: the last of the old pier is gone. He did not expect anyone to read it.

Two years later the council voted to close the harbour office and move the register to a storage unit on the ring road. A clerk from the city came to collect the ledgers in three cardboard boxes. She stacked them in the boot of her car without asking a single question about what they contained, and Elias stood on the pavement and watched her drive away.

That evening he walked out along the new pier. The lamps on the rail came on one after another, and the water below was black and flat. He stayed long enough to see the ferry round the headland and fade into the mist, then he turned and went back to the village, and he did not look behind him again.

The cabin had stood above the lake since before the road was cut through the pines, and for all those years the family had measured the seasons by what could be seen from its porch. In March the ice went out with a sound like a door closing somewhere underground, and the loons came back to the shallow bays. By June the blackflies had arrived in clouds, and the children wore long sleeves in the heat rather than surrender their arms to them. The garden went in late, as it always did, and the beans came up crooked between the stones.

My grandfather kept a ledger of the weather, one line for every day, written in pencil so that mistakes could be corrected and second thoughts recorded in the margin. He noted the first frost, the depth of the snow at the fencepost, the night the wind took the shingles off the woodshed. The ledger is in the bottom drawer of the desk now, and nobody has written in it since the autumn he stopped walking down to the dock.

The dock itself went first. A spring freshet carried away two of its sections, and he pulled the rest out with the tractor and stacked it behind the shed, saying he would rebuild it when his knees were better. He never did. The rowboat stayed upside down on sawhorses until the canvas rotted through, and then it was firewood, and then it was ash. That is how things went at the cabin: slowly, and then all at once, and then somebody would say we ought to fix that, and nobody would.

In July the family came up from the city, three cars and a truck, coolers wedged into the trunk, a dog that had never seen a porcupine. They swam off the rocks and argued about the water temperature and burned the sausages and told the same stories in the same order, and for a week the cabin was loud again. On the last night they built a fire in the pit by the water and sat around it until the wood ran out.

By then there was only the birch left, and it was green. He sent the boys down to the woodpile with the wheelbarrow and told them to bring up whatever they could find, and they came back with an armload of kindling and a great deal of argument about whose turn it was to carry the axe. The fire burned hot and fast and was gone before the marshmallows were properly charred. Someone asked whether there was more, and he said no, that was the last of the firewood, and they would have to make do with the blankets and the sound of the water.

Nobody said much after that. The loons called from the far shore, and the smoke went straight up in the still air, and one by one people went inside, until it was only the two of them left on the bench, watching the coals go grey. In the morning the cars were packed and the dog was found asleep under the porch, and he stood at the end of the drive and waved goodbye until the last of them had turned the corner onto the highway.

The ferry left the harbour at first light, and for a long while the coastline refused to settle into anything familiar. A low band of cloud hung over the water, and the islands ahead appeared and disappeared with the rhythm of the swell. I stood at the rail with a paper cup of coffee, watching a pair of gulls follow the wake. The deck smelled of diesel and salt, and the benches under the awning were wet with spray. Nobody spoke. A crewman in a yellow jacket moved along the row of cars, checking the lashings with the flat patience of a man who had done the same thing every morning for twenty years.

By the time the sun broke through, the boat was threading a channel between two wooded headlands. The eastern shore was steep and close, and the trees came down almost to the tideline; the western shore lay farther off, blurred by mist. The captain's voice came over the speaker, naming the channel and the depth of the water beneath the keel, then went quiet again. We passed a lighthouse on a bare rock, its paint blistered and its windows boarded, and a small grey house beside it with a fence that had fallen away at one end. The tide slid under the hull and the engine note changed.

For most of the crossing the islands remained empty, or seemed to. Once a fishing boat crossed our bow, trailing a line of orange floats, and the crewman raised a hand in greeting. The islands support a handful of hardy plants, such as sea thrift and campion, that cling to the rock above the spray line, and in June the slopes turn pink and white for a few weeks. There are rabbits too, though nobody on the boat could say how they got there. The guidebook in my bag devoted three pages to the history of the settlement on the largest island and one paragraph to the rest. I read the paragraph twice.

The settlement, when it appeared, was smaller than the guidebook suggested: a cluster of white houses around a stone pier, a church with a slate roof, and a shed where the ferry's mail was stacked in orange crates. A woman in a raincoat met the boat and took the crates one by one in a wheelbarrow. The streets were narrow enough that a car would have filled them, and there were no cars. The harbour wall was built of blocks of dark stone, each one marked with a number, and the numbers ran out at seventy-three. A noticeboard beside the pier advertised a ceilidh on Friday, a lost dog, and a meeting about the future of the school.

I walked up the hill behind the houses. The road became a track, and the track became a path through bracken and heather. From the top the whole archipelago was visible at once: the ferry diminishing to the south, the low green shapes of the other islands, and beyond them the open sea. The wind was strong and steady, and the grass bent away from it as if combed. I sat on a stone wall and ate the sandwich I had bought at the terminal. The bread was stale and the cheese had warmed in the sun, but the view was worth the climb.

On the way down I met an old man carrying a bucket of mussels. He had lived on the island all his life, he said, and his father before him. The population had fallen from four hundred to eighty in his lifetime, and the school now had nine pupils. The young people left for the mainland and did not come back. He did not say this with any bitterness; it was simply the way things were. He asked where I was from, and when I told him he nodded as though he had expected it. The ferry would leave again at six, he said, and it would not wait.

The weather turned in the afternoon. A squall came down the sound, and the rain drove against the windows of the waiting room in long grey sheets. The ferry appeared out of the murk an hour late, its lights blurred and its horn sounding twice. We loaded in a hurry, and the deck was cold and wet. The crossing back was rough, and most of the passengers stayed below, sleeping or staring at their phones. I stood at the stern and watched the island shrink until it was only a smudge on the horizon, then nothing. By the time the mainland lights came up, the rain had stopped and the sky was clear again.

The Quiet Return of the Kelp

For thirty years the cove behind the point was known to local divers as a graveyard. Where bull kelp had once formed a canopy thick enough to slow a boat, there was only a carpet of purple urchins and bare rock. The change happened quickly, the way these things often do: a wasting disease removed the sea stars that preyed on the urchins, the urchins multiplied, and the kelp disappeared. By the time anyone thought to count, the forest was gone.

The restoration project began with a survey that nobody expected to amount to much. A team of biologists, working with two fishing associations and a handful of volunteers, mapped the remaining patches of kelp along forty kilometres of coast. They found less than they had feared and more than they had hoped: a few pockets in deep water, sheltered from the worst of the swell, where the holdfasts still clung to the rock. These pockets became the seed stock for everything that followed.

The method they settled on was low-tech by design. Divers collected reproductive tissue from the surviving plants and brought it to a shed on the pier, where it was cultured in tanks of cold seawater under banks of fluorescent lights. When the tissue was ready, it was wrapped around small stones and dropped over the side in weighted frames. The frames were placed by hand, one at a time, along the edge of the old bed. It was slow work, and in the first winter storms carried away half of them.

The second year was better. The surviving frames held, and by spring the stones were covered in a brown fringe that the divers photographed every fortnight. The project's budget was small, and most of it went to fuel and dive gear. The shed was lent by the harbour authority, and the tanks were built from plywood and pond liner. A local school adopted one of the frames and sent drawings of the fish the children hoped to see. The drawings were pinned to the wall beside the dive log, and by the end of the season several of the species on them had actually appeared. The children were more impressed by the sea otters, which were on none of the drawings and which nobody had expected so close to shore.

Not everyone was pleased. Some commercial urchin divers argued that the restoration was simply moving the problem from one part of the coast to another, and that the kelp would return on its own if the urchins were harvested harder. The biologists disagreed, politely and in writing. The dispute was aired at a public meeting in the community hall, where the two sides sat on opposite sides of the aisle and the moderator kept a running tally of how often each speaker used the word balance. In the end the funding was renewed for another three years, with a clause requiring an independent review.

The review, published last autumn, was cautious. It noted that the kelp beds were still small relative to their historical extent, and that a single warm summer could undo much of the work. It also noted that the project had cost far less than a comparable restoration effort elsewhere, and that most of the money had stayed in the community. The recommendation was to continue, expand the survey, and stop calling the site a graveyard in official documents.

By the fifth summer the kelp had reached the surface in three places. The fronds lay flat on the water at low tide, and from the cliff above, the bed read as a single dark shape spreading north. The team began to count what came back. Urchins were still present, but their numbers had fallen where the kelp was thickest, and the fish were returning on their own. A survey in August recorded fourteen species, including the kelp perch, the painted greenling and the blue rockfish, sheltering among the fronds. None of them had been planted. They had simply found the habitat.

The project is not finished, and the people running it are careful not to say that it will be. The cove is warmer than it was, the storms are stronger, and the urchins are still there, waiting. But for the first time in a generation the surface of the bay is broken by fronds, and the divers who once called the place a graveyard now bring visitors to see it.

Chronic pain is one of the most common reasons adults seek medical care, and for three decades clinicians in North America and Europe responded by prescribing increasingly potent analgesics. The rationale seemed straightforward: pain is under-treated, these drugs relieve pain, therefore more prescribing means less suffering. By the mid-2010s, however, it had become clear that the strategy carried costs that had not been anticipated in the trials that supported it. Patients who received long courses of therapy developed tolerance, needing higher doses for the same relief, and a substantial minority developed physiological dependence. When prescriptions were stopped abruptly, withdrawal symptoms, including agitation, sweating, gastrointestinal distress, and a pervasive sense of dysphoria, drove many patients to seek supplies elsewhere. Meanwhile, the drug supply itself changed. Illicitly manufactured tablets, pressed to resemble legitimate pharmaceuticals and often containing fentanyl or other synthetic compounds far more potent than heroin, entered recreational markets. Overdose deaths climbed year after year, first among middle-aged adults with chronic pain, then among younger people who had never held a prescription. Public health agencies responded with prescription monitoring programmes, dosing guidelines, and educational campaigns aimed at primary care. Emergency departments were encouraged to offer alternatives: physical therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy, nerve blocks, and non-pharmacological pain management. Yet access to those alternatives remained uneven, and many patients who had relied on medication for years found themselves tapered against their wishes, sometimes with little support. Researchers, meanwhile, debated how much of the crisis reflected the pharmacology of the drugs themselves and how much reflected prescribing patterns, marketing, and the social conditions in which addiction takes hold. Longitudinal studies suggested that most people prescribed a short course after surgery never developed a problem, while a small but identifiable subgroup escalated rapidly. Genetic and clinical predictors of that subgroup remained elusive. The policy debate turned on questions of balance: how to keep effective analgesia available to patients who benefit while reducing exposure among those at risk. Clinicians were advised to reassess frequently, to use the lowest effective dose, and to co-prescribe naloxone for patients at elevated risk of respiratory depression. Pharmacies installed take-back programmes. State legislatures debated limits on initial prescriptions. What had once been a narrow technical question about receptor pharmacology became a broad public argument about medicine, regulation, and the responsibility of manufacturers. By the end of the decade, the leading cause of injury death in the United States was no longer motor vehicle collision but opioid overdose, and the phrase had entered ordinary conversation.

Mara inherited her grandmother's sourdough starter in a chipped mason jar, a bubbling culture older than she was. Each morning she fed it with stone-milled rye flour and filtered water, watching it rise and fall like a slow tide. She kept a notebook of feeding ratios, hydration levels, and kitchen temperatures, noting how winter slowed everything down. Her neighbor, a retired baker, taught her to judge readiness by the float test, dropping a spoonful into water to see if it bobbed. They debated the merits of autolyse, of long cold retards in the refrigerator, of scoring with a lame versus a serrated knife. Over months she learned the smell of a hungry culture, sharp with acetone, versus a ripe one, sweet and yeasty with a hint of yogurt. She baked through failures: dense bricks, gummy crumbs, loaves that spread flat across the baking stone. Friends received her experiments wrapped in linen, each loaf labeled with flour blend and bake time. She ground fresh wheat berries in a countertop mill, sifting bran for porridge and keeping the rest for dough. Summer brought new variables, fruit flies hovering over the jar, the kitchen too warm, the dough proofing in half the expected time. She adjusted by feeding at midnight, by chilling flour, by retarding shaped loaves for eighteen hours. The local miller saved her a sack of heritage Turkey Red wheat, and she shared starter with three neighbors, each naming their jar. Her oven, an old gas model with hot spots, forced her to rotate loaves and tent them with foil. She learned to steam with a cast-iron pan of lava rocks, to slash boldly, to wait a full day before slicing. The crumb turned open and custardy, holes glistening, crust crackling as it cooled on a wire rack. Market customers asked for her recipe, but she only smiled and offered them a bit of starter instead. Winter returned, and with it the slow rhythm of feeding, folding, shaping, and baking. Through every season the jar on her counter kept its quiet, ancient rhythm of slow fermentation.

Learning algebra is often described as learning a new language, and the comparison is apt in more ways than teachers usually admit. Students begin with words, describing patterns such as doubling a number or adding a fixed amount each time. Only later do they compress those descriptions into symbols, and that compression is where many of them stumble. The purpose of this chapter is to slow the transition down and to show that symbolic notation is not an arbitrary code but a compact record of operations that can be carried out in a definite order. Readers who have struggled with algebra before should not be discouraged by the pace, because the examples are deliberately short and each one is followed by a worked solution that can be checked line by line.

The first section reviews the order of operations with simple numerical examples. Students practice evaluating parenthesized expressions such as 3 × (4 + 5) - 6 / 2, then expressions that mix multiplication and division, and finally expressions that combine several operations at once. None of these exercises involves letters yet. The goal is fluency with ordinary arithmetic so that later symbolic work does not stall on basic computation.

The second section introduces the idea of an unknown quantity. A letter stands in for a number that has not yet been determined, and the surrounding notation records what is known about it. Students learn to translate sentences into equations. For instance, the sentence five more than twice a number is seventeen becomes 2x + 5 = 17, and students check that x = 6 satisfies it. By the end of the section they can write an equation from a short word problem and verify a proposed solution.

The third section turns to factoring, which is the first place where the compactness of symbolic notation really matters. Consider the equation 6x^2 - 11x + 4 = 0. The coefficient of the squared term is six, the constant is four, and the middle coefficient is negative eleven. Two numbers, negative three and negative four, multiply to give the product of six and four while summing to negative eleven, so the expression factors as (3x - 4)(2x - 1) = 0. Setting each factor equal to zero gives the two solutions, x = 4/3 and x = 1/2. Students are asked to verify both solutions by substitution and to explain why no other factor pair works.

The final section explains why factoring does not always work and previews the quadratic formula, which is derived in the next chapter. The emphasis throughout is on reading the notation carefully, one operation at a time, and on connecting each symbol back to the operation it records. Students who finish the chapter should be able to look at a compact expression and say aloud what operations it contains and in what order those operations are applied.

My first week at the literary agency was spent reading contracts, and the one I remember best belonged to a debut novelist who had clearly not read the fine print. She had come to London from Kuala Lumpur with a manuscript about a man returning to a city he no longer recognised, and the agency had sold it in three days for a sum that made the senior partners stop talking about anything else. The editor explained over lunch that the terms were unusually strict: no part of the book could be reproduced in any form, electronic or mechanical, without the express written permission of the publisher, and even the cover art had been licensed separately from the text. She laughed about it, but the author had already signed, and there was nothing anyone could do.

What struck me was how ordinary the whole conversation felt. A clause that appears in thousands of books was being discussed over sandwiches, as if it were a detail of the weather. Later I looked it up in the archive and found the same sentence in a dozen other contracts, always buried on the third or fourth page. The authors never read it. They were thinking about the cover, the tour, the review in the Sunday papers. Nobody imagines that the sentence will matter until a rights dispute arrives, and by then the lunch is long over and the editor has moved to another house.

I kept a copy of that contract for years, not because of the clause but because of the handwriting in the margin, which belonged to an agent who had died the previous winter. She had represented poets in the 1970s and had a reputation for refusing advances that were too large. The clause outlasted her, as clauses do. When the agency finally closed, the files went into storage somewhere in Essex, and I sometimes wonder whether the sentence is still there, on the third or fourth page, waiting for a reader who will never come.

Years later I saw the author at a festival in Edinburgh. She had published two more novels and had stopped reading her contracts altogether, trusting an agent she had met at a party. We talked about the first book, and she said the only thing she remembered from that spring was the cover, which she had hated. She did not remember the lunch, or the editor, or the sentence. I did not remind her. It seemed unkind, and besides, the sentence was still doing its work, quietly, in editions she would never see. Tourists bought the book in airports. Students cited it in essays. Somewhere a permissions request was being drafted, and somewhere else an assistant was checking whether the clause allowed a quotation of four hundred words or only three hundred.

Over the last two quarters the exchange has grown from twelve to forty venues, and the operations team has asked us to explain why the latency budget keeps slipping during the opening auction. This memo summarizes the measurements we collected between January and March, describes the changes we made to the deployment, and lists the questions we still cannot answer.

We instrumented every gateway node with the same tracing library and sampled one request in twenty, which produced roughly ninety million spans per day. After filtering out health checks and synthetic probes, about four fifths of the remaining traffic consisted of limit orders, while cancellations and amendments made up the rest. The busiest hour was always the first hour after the open, when order rates rose by a factor of six and queue depths along the ingest path grew faster than the autoscaler could react. We added two extra partitions to the inbound topic in February and moved the matching workers onto dedicated hosts, which removed most of the noisy-neighbor complaints from the support queue.

Traders reported that the blotter refreshed slowly whenever they switched between accounts, and after some digging we found that each account switch rebuilt the entire position table from scratch. Caching the table per session, keyed on the account identifier, removed almost all of that redundant work. We shipped the change behind a flag on the fourteenth and rolled it out to all desks by the end of the month. No incidents were attributed to the rollout, although two desks asked for the old behavior back during the first week and were told to wait for the next release.

Support tickets told a similar story. Most weeks the queue stayed empty, but the two days after each release brought a burst of questions about the new screens, and the team answered them from a shared document that slowly drifted out of date. We have since moved that document into the repository and asked the release manager to review it before every deployment, which has cut the number of repeated questions by roughly half.

On the storage side, the archive team migrated the historical trade repository to a columnar format and reported a fourfold reduction in disk usage. The migration spanned three scheduled maintenance windows, mostly because the verification jobs had to re-read every partition and compare checksums against the original files. Minutes of the Riverside planning committee, third session

The chair opened the meeting at seven and reminded members that the developer's revised drawings had been circulated on Friday, along with a letter from the residents' association and a summary of the drainage study. Six members were present, one seat was empty, and the recording secretary took notes for the file.

Mr. Alvarez presented the revised plan for the former warehouse site. The proposal now includes forty-two apartments, a small grocery on the ground floor, and a courtyard that opens onto Mill Street. The applicant has agreed to widen the sidewalk along the north edge and to plant eleven trees, though the species has not been settled. Several members asked about parking, and the applicant's engineer explained that the garage would hold fifty cars, with bicycle racks beside the loading bay.

Ms. Chen, speaking for the residents' association, said the neighborhood supported the housing but objected to the height of the eastern wing. She noted that the afternoon sun would be blocked from the community garden, that the windows of the townhouses on Alder Lane would look straight into the new stairwell, and that the delivery trucks would arrive before the school buses. The applicant offered to lower the eastern wing by one story and to move the loading bay to the rear, subject to a review by the fire marshal, who has not yet responded to the revised drawings.

A lengthy discussion followed about the drainage study. The consultant explained that the site sits on clay, that the existing culvert is undersized, and that a detention pond would be needed at the southern corner. The cost of the pond, she estimated, would fall on the developer, although the maintenance agreement would bind the city for twenty years. Mr. Okafor asked whether the pond could double as a playground, and the consultant said the slope made that impractical. The committee asked for a written opinion before the next session.

Two members asked about the timeline for the traffic study, which the city's consultant has promised for the end of the quarter. The chair said the study would be paid from the ward's discretionary fund, that the results would be posted on the committee's page, and that residents would have thirty days to comment. Ms. Chen asked whether the comment period could be extended through the holidays, and the chair agreed to consider it.

The meeting returned to the matter of the trees. Ms. Chen's association had collected signatures in favor of preserving the two mature oaks near the entrance, and the applicant's landscape architect confirmed that both could be kept if the driveway were shifted six feet to the east. That shift, however, would affect the property line and require a variance. The committee voted five to one to request the variance application and to postpone the final decision until the surveyor's report arrives.

Before adjourning, the chair read a short statement thanking the clerk for her work during the budget season, and the members agreed to meet again on the second Tuesday of next month.

By the middle of the decade the question had stopped being academic. Three circuits had already split on whether a seller who merely facilitated a transaction could be treated as a manufacturer for purposes of the statute, and the practical consequences of the split were large enough that insurers had begun writing exclusions into policies in anticipation of the answer. The panel that finally took the issue en banc was, by its own account, uneasy about the invitation. It had declined two earlier petitions presenting the same question, and the order granting the third gave no reasons at all, which the bar read as a sign that the judges themselves did not yet agree on how the argument should be framed.

The panel began with the text. It noted that the operative phrase had been carried forward without amendment since the Reconstruction era, and that nearly every court to have construed it in the interim had read the governing verb narrowly. Where Congress had meant to reach the conduct alleged here, the panel said, it had used a different formulation in adjacent sections, and the difference could not be dismissed as stylistic. The court cited, among others, Camden County Board of Chosen Freeholders v. Beretta U.S.A. Corp., 273 F.3d 536, 540 (3d Cir. 2001), and Read v. Town of Mount Hope, 412 F. Supp. 2d 288, 295 (S.D.N.Y. 2005), for the proposition that a defendant must have exercised actual control over the instrumentality before liability will attach. Neither decision, the panel conceded, was strictly binding, but the reasoning of both had been followed widely enough that departing from it would require more than a plausible alternative reading.

The dissenting judges would have gone the other way. Their objection was not so much to the panel's reading of the words as to its confidence that the words still carried the meaning they had when they were written. Language drifts, the dissent observed, and a term of art that once described a narrow class of merchants may, after a century of use, describe a much wider one. The majority's approach, on this view, treated the dictionary as a constitution and left the statute fixed at the moment of enactment while the world around it changed.

The panel answered that the argument proved too much. If the meaning of every inherited phrase were permitted to drift with the usage of the day, no commercial statute would survive a generation, and the reliance interests that such statutes create would be impossible to protect. The legislature is free to amend when it wishes, and it has done so many times in neighbouring provisions without touching this one. Silence of that kind, sustained across repeated revisions of the surrounding text, is ordinarily taken as acquiescence in the settled reading, and the panel saw no reason to treat this instance differently.

It is true that the statute's remedial purpose counsels against a construction so tight that its protections become illusory. But purpose, the panel said, is a guide for resolving genuine ambiguity, not a licence to rewrite a provision that the legislature has left untouched. The dissent's parade of horribles, that manufacturers will escape liability by interposing a shell entity between themselves and the point of sale, was met with the observation that the plaintiffs in this very case had sued the upstream manufacturer directly, and had needed to plead nothing more than the relationship and the control it implied. The judgment of the district court was affirmed, and the mandate issued in due course.

The move began badly and got worse in the ordinary way. We had booked a van for eight in the morning, but the rental office on the ring road did not open until nine, and by the time the keys were in my hand the morning traffic had already filled the slip road with cars that would not let anything larger than a bicycle merge. The flat we were leaving was on the fourth floor of a building whose lift had been out of service since the spring, so every box came down the stairwell two at a time, passed hand to hand between the four of us, and stacked in a loading bay where rain had been getting in through a broken pane for what looked like years.

We counted 63 boxes at the end, plus a rolled rug, a broken chair, and a lamp that nobody wanted but nobody would throw away either. The van was rated for 14 cubic metres, which sounded generous until the sofa went in sideways and took up a third of the space. Between the four of us we had perhaps six hours before the van had to be back, and the drive across town was 212 kilometres of motorway and then a long stretch of single carriageway where the roadworks had been going on since the previous winter and where a temporary limit of 50 applied for most of the way.

We stopped once for fuel, at a service station where the price board said 349.9 and the coffee machine accepted cards but not the card I had. Two of the movers had sandwiches in a cool bag; the rest of us had crisps and a packet of biscuits that had been in the glovebox since the last trip. The satnav took us off the motorway one junction too early, so we spent 25 minutes threading through a village with a bridge too low for the van, reversing in a pub car park to the amusement of the lunchtime drinkers.

The new place was easier in every respect except the stairs. There were 18 steps to the first landing and another 14 to the second, and the boxes that had come down two at a time went up one at a time, which is the arithmetic of moving houses and nobody has ever found a way around it. By four in the afternoon the kitchen was in, the beds were assembled, and the kettle had been found in the box marked fragile, which is where nobody had thought to look. The neighbour on the ground floor knocked to say that the water from our washing machine had been running down his wall since lunchtime, and that he had put a bucket under it and would appreciate a plumber before the weekend.

What remains is the sorting: 11 bags of paper for recycling, a drawer of cables that fit nothing we still own, and a box of photographs, which we sat on the floor and went through until it was dark. The van went back at half past seven with 40 minutes to spare, and the man at the rental office said we were the third family that day to bring it back with the fuel light on.

Inquiry into the loss of the steam trawler Ben Vane opened at the Custom House in Leith on the fourteenth of March and ran, with two adjournments, over nine sitting days. The vessel was a steel-hulled trawler of one hundred and twelve tons gross register, built at Beverley in 1897 and employed on the North Sea grounds for eleven years without any recorded incident of consequence. Evidence was led on the condition of her boilers, the sufficiency of her life-saving equipment, the competence of the watch kept during the hours before the foundering, and the accuracy of the survey certificates issued to her in the preceding autumn. The assessor, Mr Hume, appeared for the Board of Trade; the owners were represented by Mr Laing of Leith; and the families of the six hands who were lost were represented, at the court's own direction and at no expense to them, by Mr Balfour.

The harbourmaster was heard first. He described the weather on the night in question as squally, with a heavy swell running from the north-east and the glass falling steadily since the middle of the afternoon. He told the court that no warning had been issued to the fleet, the season being an ordinary one and the forecast giving no indication of anything out of the common way. Pressed by the assessor on the point, he allowed that the forecast had been amended at seven o'clock and that the amendment had reached his office some twenty minutes later, by which time most of the fleet was already at sea.

The engine fitter who had serviced the vessel in January was next examined. He spoke to the state of the feed pumps and to a repair to the starboard injector that had been carried out at the owners' request and not, in his view, because the injector was dangerous. He agreed that he had noted a weeping joint on the main steam pipe and that he had drawn it to the attention of the second engineer, whose duty it was to report it to the skipper. He could not say whether that had been done, and he was not pressed further.

A retired skipper, called as an expert, gave it as his opinion that the vessel would have shipped very little water had the hatches been properly secured, and that the speed with which she went down pointed to an opening in the hull below the waterline rather than to any failure of the pumps. He was inclined to attribute the loss to contact with floating wreckage of the kind reported by the second hand, though he conceded under questioning that no such wreckage had been recovered and that the report might have been mistaken.

The court then heard from the mate, who had served under the same skipper since 1908 and who was the senior survivor. He described the sequence of the night with care, correcting himself twice as to the hour. Asked by the assessor whether the crew had received any warning of the approaching squall, he replied without hesitation "Sure, we had the glass falling all afternoon and every man aboard knew what it meant."

Counsel for the owners put it to him that the hatch covers had been inspected that same morning and found sound, and the mate agreed that they had been inspected, though he would not go further than that.

Reservoir levels in the northern basin have fallen faster this year than at any point since records began, according to the regional water authority, and officials are preparing to impose the first mandatory restrictions in more than a decade.

The authority's monthly bulletin shows the main reservoir at 28 per cent of capacity, down from 61 per cent a year ago. Two smaller reservoirs that feed the irrigation network are effectively empty, and water has been trucked to farms above the line of the main canal since early summer. Recording began in 1954, and the current level is the lowest for the date since 1994, when restrictions were last imposed. That episode lasted eleven months and was lifted only after two consecutive wet winters.

Farmers in the valley say the restrictions will reach them first. "We can survive one dry year and maybe two," said Elena Marchetti, who grows apricots on forty hectares near the canal. "Nobody here is arguing about whether the climate is changing. We are arguing about who gets the water that is left."

Industrial users account for about a fifth of demand, and the largest of them, a bottling plant outside the town, has already cut its intake voluntarily. The authority says it will not exempt any user from the cap, although it has discretion to grant temporary relief in cases of hardship, a provision that has been used twice in thirty years.

A question of timing

The restrictions would take effect in stages, beginning with limits on garden watering and the washing of vehicles, and ending with a cap on the volume that farms may draw from the canal. Households would be asked to cut consumption by 15 per cent, with higher tariffs for those who exceed the limit. The authority's chair said the board had tried to avoid mandatory measures. "We have asked, we have advertised, we have written to every ratepayer twice," she said. "Voluntary savings have plateaued at about six per cent. We cannot get to fifteen by asking."

Not everyone on the board agrees. Two of the seven members argued at the last meeting for a delay, on the grounds that the autumn rains may yet arrive. The authority's own hydrologists put the chance of a normal season at less than one in four.

Early life

Hollis was born in a farmhouse two miles inland, the eldest of four children. His father was a boatbuilder and his mother kept the accounts for a family business that traded in salt and dried fish along the coast.

He attended the parish school until he was thirteen and was then apprenticed to a sailmaker in the neighbouring town. The water stood lower than the previous year, and in several places the mud had dried into pale polygons with salt crusts along the cracks. A pair of ducks circled the second pond twice before settling in the far corner.

By mid-morning the fog had burned off and the light turned harsh. We ate lunch on the tailgate of the truck while a tractor worked a field beyond the levee, raising a line of dust that drifted slowly north. The technician checked the sensors and found that two of them had been pulled loose by muskrats during the week; she spliced the cables, sealed the housings, and wrote a long note in the maintenance log.

The afternoon was spent measuring the outflow channel, which had cut a new bank on the western side. The current ran stronger than expected, and the gauge had to be anchored twice before it held. In the reed beds the wind made a dry rustling that never quite stopped, and once a small plane passed low enough that we could read the numbers under its wing.

The museum staff had asked for a short summary of the day's counts, so we sketched the route on a map and marked the places where erosion had undercut the bank. Later, at the office, the numbers went into a spreadsheet that someone would turn into a chart for the annual report, and the photographs were filed under the names of the ponds.

On the way back we walked the same boardwalk, now crowded with visitors carrying cameras. The tide had come in and the channels were full, reflecting a sky that had turned the color of old pewter. At the first overlook a new interpretive sign carried the line we had copied into the notebook that morning: The heron returned to the same shallow pool before sunrise. Nobody spoke for a moment. Then we packed the gear, checked the gate, and drove out along the levee road before the light failed.

The Luberon is a low mountain range in the south of France, and the villages along its southern flank have been drawing visitors for a century and a half, ever since the railways made Avignon an easy day's journey from Paris. What follows is a short account of a week spent walking between them, mostly on the network of old mule tracks that the communes still maintain, and occasionally on the narrower paths the shepherds use when they move their flocks up to the summer pastures in June.

The first two days were spent in the valley. The heat in the afternoons was considerable, and the cicadas, which had begun singing in earnest in the last week of June, made the middle of the day almost impossible for walking; we learned to start at six, to stop by eleven, and to take the long lunch that the region has organised its whole life around. The market at Apt, on a Tuesday, is the largest in the Vaucluse, and it is worth arriving early if you want to buy cheese from the producers themselves rather than from the wholesalers who take the stalls in the square by nine. We bought a great deal of cheese, more than two people could reasonably eat, and carried most of it to the next village in a canvas bag that soon smelled of it permanently.

The walks are not difficult, though they are steep. The limestone here is soft and pale, and the paths have been worn into it over centuries, so that in places you seem to be walking in a shallow channel, a gutter of stone that holds the heat long after the sun has gone behind the ridge. The vegetation is the familiar Provencal mixture: holm oak, juniper, thyme, lavender in the fields that are still farmed, and a great deal of broom, which in early summer covers the hillsides in yellow and smells, on a hot afternoon, faintly of vanilla. There are lizards on every wall and, on one memorable occasion, a snake crossing the path ahead of us at considerable speed; it was, we later established, a Montpellier snake, harmless, though it did not feel harmless at the time.

Evenings were spent in the squares. Each village has one, and each square has a plane tree, and under the plane tree there are chairs, and the chairs are occupied from about six o'clock by men who appear to have been there since the morning. The light at that hour is the reason people come here, and no photograph does it justice. Dinner, in the villages, is served at seven or at half past seven, and consists of whatever the market offered that morning, cooked simply and served outdoors, usually with a great deal of bread and a bottle of the local rose, which is pale and dry and goes down far too easily.

The villages themselves differ from one another more than the guidebooks suggest. Some are built of the pale limestone of the ridge, some of the red and ochre clays of the western edge, and one or two have grown so used to visitors that the shop windows are given over entirely to lavender bags and postcards. It is easy, and perhaps a little unfair, to complain about this; the alternative, for villages this small and this far from any industry, is usually abandonment, and the same shops keep the bakery and the butcher alive for the people who live there through the winter. We tried to buy something every day, if only a coffee, and to eat where the menu was written in French.

On the last morning we walked up to the ridge above the valley, and from the top, with the mist still lying in the folds of the hills, you could see the whole chain of them, one after another, each on its own outcrop of rock, each with its square tower or its castle ruin.
