Elena woke before the sun and lay still for a while, listening to the wind move through the trees outside her window. She had not slept well. The letter on the table was still there, of course, exactly where she had left it the night before, and she had read it enough times to know every word by heart. It said little. It said that the writer was sorry, that the decision had been difficult, and that everyone involved wished her well. None of that helped.

She got up, dressed without thinking, and made coffee in the small kitchen. The refrigerator hummed. A bird outside repeated the same four notes, over and over, as if it had forgotten the rest of the song. She stood at the counter with the cup in both hands and watched the light change from gray to gold. There was no reason to hurry. There was nowhere she had to be.

By seven she was outside, walking along the road that led away from the village and up toward the ridge. The air was cold and clean. She passed a farmhouse where a dog barked at her from behind a fence, then a field where the grass had grown tall and gone to seed, then a gate that someone had left open. She closed it behind her. The road narrowed and began to climb.

She walked for an hour without meeting anyone. Her thoughts moved in slow circles, returning again and again to the same few moments, the same few sentences, the same expression on the same face. She tried to name what she felt and could not. It was not anger exactly, and not grief, though it had something in common with both. It was more like the feeling of standing in a room after the furniture has been carried out.

Near the top of the ridge the trees thinned and the ground turned rocky. She stopped at a place where the road bent around a large stone and sat down on the warm surface, facing the valley. Below her the fields were still green, and the river caught the light in a long, wavering line. She could see the village, small and tidy, and the roof of the house where she had grown up, and the road she had walked that morning, winding back the way she had come. Nothing had changed. That was the problem, she thought, and then laughed at herself, because it was not a problem at all.

She stayed on the ridge until the afternoon began to cool. On the way down she met a man walking a dog, and they nodded to each other without speaking. She reached the village as the light turned orange, bought bread and milk, and went home. The letter was still on the table. She put the groceries away, sat down, and read it one last time. Then she folded it carefully and put it in a drawer. Tomorrow she would start looking for an apartment, and a job, and whatever else she needed. For tonight, that was enough. She opened the window and listened to the bird repeat its four notes.

At the counter she wrote down what she needed from the store: bread, milk, coffee, batteries, and a light bulb for the hallway. Then she turned off the lamp and slept. Outside, the wind kept moving through the trees.

The old customs house stands at the bend of the river where the ferry once landed, and for most of the nineteenth century it was the busiest building in the town. Clerks recorded the cargo of every vessel that tied up below the windows, from barrels of salted fish to crates of manufactured goods bound inland. The upper floor held the offices of the harbour master, whose maps and ledgers are still kept in the county archive. When the railway arrived in 1848 the river trade declined quickly, and by 1870 the building was used mainly for storage. It changed hands several times over the next hundred years and at one point housed a small printing works, whose presses left a mark on the stone floor of the eastern wing. The town council bought the property in 1974 and opened it as a museum two years later, but the roof was repaired only in patches and the drainage was never brought up to standard. A survey in 2011 found rot in the north wall and recommended closing the upper floor, which has remained shut ever since. Visitors can still see the ground-floor exhibits, including the harbour master's desk and a collection of ships' registers, but the upper rooms and their maps are visible only in photographs. The building was listed in 1968 and appears on the council's heritage register, although the entry has never been updated to reflect the later surveys. In 2019 a local heritage trust raised a modest sum for emergency repairs, enough to stabilise the roof but not to reopen the floor above, and the trust has been negotiating with the council about the lease ever since. Volunteers catalogued the map collection during the closure, photographing each sheet and recording its condition in a spreadsheet that now runs to several thousand rows. The council's conservation officer has said that any reopening must wait until the humidity in the upper rooms can be controlled throughout the year, because the paper is brittle and the river air is damp for much of the winter.

Restoration
The present programme began in 2022 with a full structural survey and a condition report on the stonework. Work on the north wall was completed last spring, and the drainage has been replaced along the river frontage. The trust intends to reopen the upper floor once the map collection has been rehoused in climate-controlled cases.

Wastewater treatment plants combine physical, chemical and biological processes to remove contaminants from municipal and industrial effluent before it is discharged into receiving waters. The preliminary stage relies on coarse screens and grit chambers to remove large debris, rags and dense inorganic particles that would otherwise damage pumps and clog downstream pipelines. Primary clarification follows, in which suspended solids settle under gravity and are removed as primary sludge; the overflow passes to the biological train, where the organic load is reduced by activated sludge, trickling filters or, increasingly, membrane bioreactors.

Aeration basins are the working core of conventional activated sludge systems. Here, a mixed liquor of microorganisms oxidises biodegradable organic matter and, under alternating anoxic conditions, converts nitrate to nitrogen gas. Operating staff control the dissolved oxygen setpoint, the solids retention time and the internal recycle ratio, because each parameter influences both the removal efficiency and how readily the sludge settles. Bulking sludge, caused by filamentous organisms, remains one of the most persistent operational problems; it produces a poor sludge volume index, causes solids carry-over in the secondary clarifier and can ultimately breach the discharge consent. Operators therefore monitor the sludge volume index daily and adjust the food-to-microorganism ratio whenever the value drifts upward.

Chemical dosing is used at several points in the train. Ferric chloride or aluminium sulphate may be added ahead of primary clarification to improve phosphorus removal, and polymer is dosed to the thickening centrifuge to condition the sludge before dewatering. The dosing pumps are calibrated against the feed's dry solids content, and the polymer demand is determined by jar tests performed several times each week. In plants that receive industrial waste from food processing, the influent load can vary by a factor of five within a single working day, so the equalisation tank and the load-based control loops are essential to prevent shock loads from reaching the biomass.

Nutrient removal has become the dominant design objective in catchments that discharge into sensitive waters. Enhanced biological phosphorus removal depends on alternating anaerobic and aerobic zones, which select for polyphosphate-accumulating organisms. Nitrogen removal requires a sufficiently long sludge age for nitrifying bacteria to persist, together with an adequate carbon source in the anoxic zone; many plants add glycerol, acetate or a fermented primary sludge liquor when the influent carbon-to-nitrogen ratio falls below about four to one. These additions raise the chemical oxygen demand carried by the recycle stream and must be balanced against the aeration capacity, because every kilogram of added carbon ultimately demands oxygen in the aerobic zone.

Instrumentation and control have changed the way plants are operated. Online analysers for ammonia, nitrate and phosphate now provide fifteen-minute readings that drive the aeration valves and the internal recycle rates; soft sensors infer the oxygen uptake rate from airflow and pressure data; and digital twins are used to test control changes before they are implemented on the plant. Nevertheless, operators treat fault signals cautiously, because a fouled probe or a drifted calibration can trigger unnecessary changes in the biological configuration. In winter the reduced reaction rates and the colder influent make the ammonia limit the tightest constraint on the whole train.

Solids handling consumes a large share of the operating budget. Thickened sludge is dewatered to roughly twenty-five percent dry solids, and the cake is either composted, dried for agricultural use, incinerated or sent to landfill, depending on local regulation and cost. Odour control in the solids building is achieved with a packed-tower scrubber followed by an activated carbon filter.

During the most recent inspection the regulator identified several gaps in the monitoring programme, and the plant's operators ordered a detailed assessment of microbial contamination levels in the final effluent. A follow-up review is scheduled for the spring.

Five habits that make a home easier to heat

- Draught-proof the obvious gaps. Most of the heat a house loses on a winter evening escapes through the letterbox, the keyhole and the gap under the kitchen door, and a few metres of brush strip will fix all three in an afternoon.
- Insulate the loft properly. A depth of 270 mm is the current recommendation, which is usually deeper than the joists, so the insulation is laid crosswise on top of the first layer rather than pressed between the timbers.
- Let the sun do some work. South-facing glazing should be kept clean and unobstructed, and heavy curtains drawn back during the day rather than left half-closed against the light.
- Service the boiler every autumn. A well-adjusted boiler runs a few degrees cooler and a good deal more efficiently, and the engineer will usually spot a failing pump before it strands you in January.
- Treat the windows before the walls. Secondary glazing on single-glazed sashes costs far less than internal wall insulation and delivers most of the comfort improvement for a fraction of the disruption.

The energy landscape picture, developed through the 1990s, replaced the older view of a single dominant folding pathway with an ensemble of routes descending a funnel-shaped surface whose width reflects the entropy lost as structure forms. Chaperones do not supply folding information; they bind exposed hydrophobic patches on partially folded chains and thereby prevent aggregation, releasing their substrate in an ATP-dependent cycle. Every scholarly discipline has inherited a genre it rarely examines: the reference list. Its conventions are remarkably stable across fields, even where the surrounding prose is not. An entry normally opens with the responsible parties, continues with the title of the work, and closes with enough publication detail to let a reader find the thing without asking the author. Editors argue endlessly about punctuation, about whether the year belongs beside the author or at the end, about the abbreviation of journal names, and about how to treat a work with more than a dozen contributors. What is never argued is the underlying idea, which is that a claim should be traceable to a source by anyone who cares to look. The same logic governs footnotes, catalogues raisonnes, ships' logs and the schedules at the back of an annual report: order the items the same way each time, so that a reader who has learned the pattern once can scan it forever.

A county record office is rarely the product of a single act of collection. It accumulates: a solicitor's office clears its strongroom, a family sells a house and the deeds come in, a parish deposits its vestry books because the safe in the church tower has begun to leak. Each accession arrives with its own internal order, its own vocabulary of description, and its own assumptions about what future readers will want to know. The archivist's task is not to impose a single scheme but to record what each deposit contains in terms that a stranger can use, and to do so at a level of detail that neither drowns the reader nor hides the thing being described.

For the medieval and early modern material the description is usually quite compressed: a class of document, a rough count of leaves or membranes, a date or date range, and a note of how the item came to the office. Later deposits are often described in more detail, household correspondence in bundles, estate maps as individual sheets, photographs as a series with a note of the process and the photographer where it is known. The catalogue therefore looks uneven, and archivists have argued for a century about whether that unevenness is a failure of method or an honest reflection of the material itself.

A representative sequence from the Cumberland deposits reads as follows:

MS 114 - Cartulary of the priory of St Bees - parchment, 214 folios - s. xiv - deposited 1911
MS 115 - Register of the guild of St Mary, Carlisle - paper, 96 folios - 1478 - deposited 1911
MS 117 - Account roll, manor of Skelton - parchment roll, 8 membranes - 1394-95 - deposited 1923
MS 118 - Court book, barony of Greystoke - paper, 311 folios - 1521-1587 - deposited 1923
MS 121 - Survey of the honour of Cockermouth - paper, 44 folios - 1603 - deposited 1936
MS 124 - Correspondence of the Fletcher family - 12 bundles - 1712-1840 - deposited 1948
MS 126 - Maps of the river Derwent - 7 sheets, ink on vellum - c. 1760 - deposited 1948
MS 129 - Ledger of the Maryport shipyard - paper, 402 folios - 1801-1866 - deposited 1955
MS 131 - Tithe apportionment, parish of Torpenhow - 2 rolls - 1841 - deposited 1955
MS 134 - Photographs of the Keswick flood - 31 prints, gelatin silver - 1898 - deposited 1967
MS 137 - Diary of a fell shepherd - paper, 88 folios - 1922-1931 - deposited 1974
MS 140 - Minute book, Cumberland Naturalists' Society - paper, 240 folios - 1874-1912 - deposited 1980

None of these items is remarkable on its own, and a reader looking for a single document will find the formula tedious. Read as a sequence, however, the entries carry information that no individual entry contains: the shift from parchment to paper, the growing proportion of business and family records relative to ecclesiastical ones, the appearance of photography at the very end, and the plain fact that the rate of deposit accelerated sharply after the Second World War as the old estates broke up and their papers were dispersed.

This is the argument archivists make for keeping the list intact rather than breaking it into subject indexes. An index answers the question you already know how to ask. A calendar, read straight through, tells you what the office thought worth keeping, decade by decade, which is a different and often more useful kind of evidence.

Ambient air monitoring in cities has traditionally relied on a small number of fixed reference stations, each costing more than a family car and requiring mains power, climate control and regular calibration against certified gas cylinders. Because a city can afford only a handful of such sites, the picture of pollution they produce is coarse in space even when it is accurate in time, and it says almost nothing about the hotspots people actually walk through on the way to school or work. Low-cost electrochemical and optical sensors changed the economics of the problem: a unit that fits in a lunchbox can now report particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide and ozone every minute, and several hundred of them can be deployed across a city for the price of a single reference instrument. What the cheap devices gain in coverage, however, they lose in stability. Their readings drift with temperature and humidity, they respond to gases other than the one they are nominally measuring, and their response degrades as the sensing film ages, so that two identical units sitting side by side can disagree by more than the difference between a clean park and a busy junction. The usual remedy is to co-locate a subset of the low-cost units with a reference station for several weeks, fit a correction model on the overlapping period, and then apply that model to the rest of the network; the quality of the correction depends on how well the co-location period samples the range of weather the city actually experiences. Each plot is a ten-metre square, and within each plot every woody stem taller than twenty centimetres was identified to species, measured for basal diameter, and mapped.

Sampling took place over three field seasons, in late spring and again in early autumn, to capture both the spring flush and the autumn fruiting period. Because access to the northern spit depends on tide and weather, two plots were sampled only once. Observers rotated among plots to reduce individual bias, and a second observer independently re-identified ten percent of stems; disagreements were resolved in the field or, where the specimen was sterile, by reference to a herbarium collection.

Soils were sampled at five points per plot and combined into a single composite sample. Texture, organic content, pH, and exchangeable cations were measured in the university laboratory. The dominant species across all plots were a low-growing oak, a dense shrubby willow, and a mat-forming grass. Cover of the oak was highest on the older, stable dunes, while the willow expanded where sand deposition had buried stems during the previous two winters. The grass was largely confined to the seaward edge and to recent blowouts, where it appeared to stabilise loose sand before other species established.

Growth rings from the oak were used to estimate stem age. Ring counts were cross-checked against the establishment dates of the permanent plots for stems that had been tagged as seedlings at the start of the survey. Stem density increased on eleven of the sixteen plots, declined on three, and was unchanged on the remaining two. The decline on one plot followed a fire that burned roughly a third of the plot in the second field season.

Leaf and stem specimens were collected from five individuals of each dominant species per plot. Leaf area, leaf thickness, and trichome density were measured on ten fully expanded leaves per individual. Specimens were dried and weighed, and the resulting values were expressed per unit leaf area.

Plasma samples were thawed on ice and vortexed for thirty seconds before aliquots of 50 microlitres were transferred to polypropylene tubes. Protein precipitation was carried out by adding 150 microlitres of ice-cold acetonitrile containing the internal standard at a concentration of 200 nanograms per millilitre. The mixtures were vortexed for two minutes and centrifuged at 14,000 g for ten minutes at 4 degrees Celsius. The supernatant was diluted twofold with water and 2 microlitres were injected onto the analytical column.

Chromatographic separation was achieved on a C18 column (2.1 by 50 millimetres, 1.8 micrometre particle size) maintained at 40 degrees Celsius. The mobile phase consisted of 0.1 percent formic acid in water (A) and 0.1 percent formic acid in acetonitrile (B), delivered at a flow rate of 0.4 millilitres per minute. A gradient was applied from 5 percent to 95 percent B over 3.5 minutes, held for 0.5 minutes, and returned to initial conditions for a further 1.5 minutes to allow re-equilibration. Detection was performed on a triple quadrupole mass spectrometer operating in positive electrospray ionisation mode with the capillary voltage set to 3.5 kilovolts and the source temperature at 500 degrees Celsius.

Multiple reaction monitoring transitions were optimised by infusing a 1 microgram per millilitre standard solution. The quantifier transition was m/z 342.1 to 128.0 and the qualifier transition was m/z 342.1 to 156.1; the collision energies were 22 and 30 electron volts respectively. Nitrogen was used as the collision gas at a pressure of 4.5 millitorr. Peak integration was performed by the instrument software with manual review of every chromatogram, and a signal-to-noise ratio of at least 10 was required for a peak to be accepted as valid.

Calibration standards were prepared in blank plasma at eight concentrations spanning 1 to 1000 nanograms per millilitre. The calibration curve was fitted by weighted least squares with a weighting factor of 1/x squared, and linearity was accepted when the coefficient of determination exceeded 0.99 and every back-calculated standard fell within 15 percent of its nominal value, except at the lower limit of quantification, where 20 percent was permitted. Accuracy and precision were assessed on three validation days with six replicates at each of four concentration levels. Within-run precision ranged from 2.1 to 6.8 percent and between-run precision from 3.4 to 9.2 percent. Mean accuracy was between 92 and 108 percent across the validation range. Stability was demonstrated for 24 hours at room temperature, for three freeze-thaw cycles, and for six weeks at minus 80 degrees Celsius.

The extraction recovery was determined by comparing the peak areas of extracted samples with those of post-extraction spiked samples at three concentrations. Recovery was between 88 and 94 percent, and the internal standard showed comparable behaviour, which compensates for variation introduced during sample preparation. Matrix effects were evaluated in six individual lots of blank plasma by calculating the matrix factor as the ratio of the peak area in the presence of matrix to that in neat solution, corrected by the internal standard. The corrected matrix factor varied between 0.94 and 1.06, indicating the absence of a significant ion suppression effect across the lots tested.

The idea of lighting the point had been raised, and dismissed, at least three times before anyone put money behind it. In 1868 a shipping clerk named Aldous Pike wrote to the harbour board describing how a schooner had run aground within sight of the town on a clear night, and how the crew had spent six hours in the water before a fishing boat happened to pass. The board thanked him for his interest and filed the letter. Two years later, after a second wreck in almost the same spot, a committee was formed, subscriptions were collected, and a design was commissioned from an engineer in the capital who had never visited the coast.

The engineer's first proposal was extravagant. It called for a tower of dressed granite, a lantern of polished brass, and a keeper's house with four rooms and a slate roof. The estimate came to more than the town raised in a year from harbour dues, and the committee, which had hoped for something modest, sent it back with a request for economies. The second proposal was cheaper and, everyone agreed afterwards, worse in almost every respect. The tower was to be built of rubble masonry faced with cement, the lantern was to be iron, and the keeper's house was reduced to two rooms and a lean-to shed. Work began in the spring of 1871 and proceeded slowly, interrupted by weather, by disputes over the quality of the stone, and by the repeated absence of the foreman, who was also the landlord of the principal inn and found that business more agreeable than building.

By the time the tower was finished, in the autumn of 1873, the cost had risen by nearly half again, and the committee had been reconstituted twice. The light was lit on the first of November, in front of a crowd of perhaps two hundred people, most of whom had come to see whether it would work. It did work. For eleven years it turned every night, and the records of the harbour board show only two complaints, both about the brightness of the beam in the windows of houses on the eastern shore.

Then, in the winter of 1884, a storm carried away the iron lantern and a considerable part of the seaward wall. The keeper, who had been in the tower at the time, survived with a broken shoulder and a lasting distrust of engineers. The board took evidence for a month. The upshot was a report of forty pages which concluded, in language of remarkable delicacy, that the cement facing had not been suited to the climate — a finding that the original engineer, who had by then retired to a house in the hills and refused to answer letters, had predicted in a footnote to his first and rejected proposal — and that the tower should be rebuilt in stone after all.

The rebuilding took three years and cost twice the original estimate. The new tower stood for sixty years, long after the fishing fleet had moved to a deeper harbour to the north, and long after the last keeper had been replaced by automatic machinery. It was demolished in 1954 to make room for a car park, and the stone was sold as building material to a contractor who used most of it for garden walls. Visitors to the town today are shown a brass plate on a bollard near the quay, which records the dates of construction and demolition and nothing at all about the arguments, the storms, or the two hundred people who came out on a November evening to see whether the light would work.

Kaltbrunn railway station serves the municipality of Kaltbrunn in the Swiss canton of St. Gallen. It lies on the Uznach to Wattwil line, close to the western portal of the long Ricken Tunnel, and is served by hourly St. Gallen S-Bahn service S4, which runs in both directions around a loop through Wattwil, St. Gallen, Sargans, Ziegelbrücke and Uznach. The station opened in 1903 with the completion of the line, and the present building dates from 1911. Freight traffic was withdrawn in the 1990s, and the goods shed was later converted into a workshop for the local bus company.

For most of its history the station was staffed, with a ticket office, a signal box and a small restaurant on the platform. Automation arrived in stages. The signal box closed in 2003, the ticket office in 2011, and the last staff member left in 2015. Passengers now buy tickets from a machine beside the entrance, and the platform is monitored by cameras. The station has two side platforms, each long enough for four coaches, connected by a pedestrian underpass that replaced the original level crossing in 1988. A footpath along the track leads to the village centre in about ten minutes.

Editors who write about Swiss railway stations have long argued about how to arrange their articles into groups. Some prefer one broad list of stations in the canton; others want finer divisions by line, by operator, by canton, or by the century in which a station opened. The argument matters because readers arrive by many routes. One reader wants a timetable, another wants the history of a tunnel, and a third wants to know which stations are served by the S4. The category system at the bottom of an article is only one of several ways of finding related pages, and it is easy to forget that the lead paragraph, the infobox and the route diagram each carry information too.

The article about Kaltbrunn was started in 2007 and has been expanded by a dozen contributors. The opening date of 1903 is repeated in the lead, in the history section and in the infobox, and the line to Wattwil is described in a separate article. A 2019 discussion about over-grouping small stations produced no firm conclusion, but several editors agreed that a short article with three or four groups is easier to maintain than one with a dozen. The station building was listed in the cantonal inventory in 2016.

The Hazel Dell Bridge carries County Road 900 north across Clear Creek in Mason County, Illinois, about four miles west of Manito. The structure has three steel truss spans resting on concrete piers, with a total length of 214 feet and a roadway 20 feet wide. It was built in 1903 by the Decatur Bridge Company for the county board, replacing a wooden covered bridge that had been damaged by ice the previous winter.

At the time of its construction the bridge carried horse traffic, wagons of grain and the occasional herd of cattle, and the county advertised it as one of the strongest crossings on the creek. The first automobiles crossed in 1907. Repairs followed floods in 1913, 1937 and 1974; the 1974 work replaced the timber deck with an open steel grate and added a railing along the southern sidewalk. A weight limit of ten tons was imposed in 1985 and lowered to six tons in 2011 after an inspection found section loss in the lower chords.

The trusses are pinned Pratt through-truss spans, a common design of the period, each 71 feet long and braced with lateral struts at the top. The original iron railings were replaced with steel ones during the 1937 repairs, and the concrete piers were faced with new stone in 2016. Engineers who surveyed the bridge in 2005 noted that the pin connections were unusually well preserved and recommended that the trusses be cleaned and repainted rather than replaced.

The nearby community of Hazel Dell was never incorporated. A school, a general store and a grain elevator served the surrounding farms until the middle of the twentieth century, and the store closed in 1962. The school building survives as a private residence, and the elevator was demolished in 1998. County road records describe the bridge as the principal crossing between Manito and the farms to the north, and school buses used it until a larger bridge was built downstream in 2002.

The bridge was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1999 for its association with early twentieth-century county bridge construction. A local preservation group nominated it after a 2005 survey of Mason County crossings, and the nomination cited the surviving original trusses and the concrete piers. The group has since raised money for a condition study and for interpretive signs at the northern approach. The county has no plans to replace the bridge, although heavy trucks are now routed to the downstream crossing, and the structure is inspected every two years.

The deep scattering layer is a broad band of marine life that rises toward the surface after sunset and sinks again before dawn. It was first detected by naval sonar operators who saw a false seafloor drifting upward on their screens. The animals responsible are mostly small fish, squid and shrimp that spend the daylight hours in dim water where predators cannot easily find them. When darkness falls they swim upward through hundreds of metres to feed on plankton near the surface. The layer is thick enough in places to reflect the sound of a survey vessel, and it can confuse echo sounders used for mapping the seabed. Researchers who study it lower nets and cameras into the migrating band and record which species appear at which depth. Because the animals are fragile, many are damaged before they reach the deck. Newer instruments photograph them in place and count them by silhouette. The nightly migration moves an enormous quantity of carbon from the surface toward the deep ocean, a service that is easy to overlook and hard to replace.

The tribunal began by recalling the principle that a person who signs a document is ordinarily bound by its terms whether or not they have read it. That principle is not absolute. It yields where the party seeking to rely on the clause knew that the signatory had been misled about its effect, and it yields more readily where the clause is unusual or onerous. The question here is whether the clause excluding liability for consequential loss was brought to the appellant's attention before the contract was formed. It follows that the exclusion cannot be relied upon and that the appeal must be allowed.

Wind moves sand along a beach in two ways. Most grains bounce along the surface in short hops and the rest drift in suspension above the ground. The bouncing grains knock other grains loose and the whole sheet creeps forward grain by grain. When the wind blows steadily from one direction the sand builds a ridge across the beach. The ridge grows until the slope on the windward side becomes too steep to hold and then it collapses. Each collapse moves the ridge a little further inland. Over a season the beach can shift many metres and a path that was clear in spring may be buried by autumn. Plants slow this movement because their roots hold the surface and their leaves break the wind. That is why a bare dune migrates while a vegetated one stays where it is. People who build too close to a shifting dune learn this slowly and expensively.

The rover crested the rim of the crater shortly after local noon, its wheels crunching over fractured bedrock that glittered under a pale butterscotch sky. Ahead lay a field of dark dunes rippled like corduroy, bordered by pale outcrops that orbital spectra suggested were rich in hydrated minerals. We left the valley town before dawn, headlamps bobbing along the cobbled lane as dogs barked behind shuttered courtyards and the first buses coughed awake in the depot. The trail climbed at once through eucalyptus groves where the air smelled of damp bark and woodsmoke, then broke onto open hillside terraced with stone walls older than anyone could remember. Our guide set a steady pace, pausing at each spring to fill bottles and point out hawks circling above the ravines. By midmorning we had gained the first pass, a windswept saddle strung with faded prayer flags that snapped and fluttered in the thin bright air. Below us the next valley opened in layered shades of green and gold, stitched with footpaths and dotted with thatched hamlets where smoke rose straight into the still sky. We descended carefully over loose scree, knees aching, until the path leveled beside a rushing stream lined with mossy boulders and tiny orchids. Lunch was bread, cheese and boiled potatoes eaten in the shade of a rock overhang while porters joked in a language we barely understood. In the afternoon the weather turned, clouds boiling over the ridge and rain sweeping down in cold grey sheets that soaked our jackets and turned the trail to mud. We pressed on through the downpour, crossing swaying footbridges and climbing stone staircases worn hollow by centuries of feet. At dusk we reached a village perched on a shoulder of the mountain, where lanterns glowed in low doorways and the smell of soup drifted from a communal kitchen. The family who hosted us spread blankets on the floor, served us thick stew with herbs we could not name, and told stories of traders, pilgrims and soldiers who had passed this way. Sleep came fast despite the altitude headache and the distant barking of dogs. The next day brought clearer skies and a gentler grade through pine forest where resin scented the air and woodpeckers hammered overhead. We passed waterfalls threading silver down black cliffs, meadows bright with lupines and asters, and herders driving shaggy cattle toward high pasture. Every turn of the path revealed another folded ridge receding toward a horizon crowned with snow. On the third morning the great peak finally showed itself, a white pyramid floating above the clouds, impossibly vast and calm. None of us spoke for a while. We simply stood at the edge of the meadow, packs slipped from tired shoulders, and watched light move across the glaciers. That evening, gathered around a small fire beneath unfamiliar stars, we agreed the blisters, the rain and the thin air had all been worth enduring for a single clear view of the mountain.

Coral reefs are among the most productive marine ecosystems, yet their persistence depends on a narrow range of environmental conditions. Reef-building corals are colonial cnidarians that host photosynthetic dinoflagellates within their gastrodermal cells. This endosymbiosis supplies the host with most of its reduced carbon, and in exchange the coral provides inorganic nutrients and a sheltered intracellular niche. Thermal stress disrupts the partnership: sustained elevations of sea surface temperature of one to two degrees Celsius above the local summer maximum trigger the expulsion of symbionts, a process known as bleaching. Bleached colonies lose pigmentation, experience reduced calcification, and may die if the anomaly persists for weeks.

Physiological studies have identified several correlates of thermal tolerance. Antioxidant capacity, heat-shock protein expression, and the composition of membrane lipids differ between bleaching-resistant and bleaching-susceptible genotypes. Molecular surveys of host and symbiont transcriptomes indicate that the stress response involves the downregulation of photosynthesis-related genes and the upregulation of innate immune pathways. Whether these transcriptional signatures are causes or consequences of bleaching remains contested.

Ocean acidification represents a second global stressor. As atmospheric carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, carbonate chemistry shifts: pH declines, the saturation state of aragonite falls, and calcifying organisms must expend more energy to precipitate skeletal material. Experimental mesocosms show that acidification reduces net calcification in many coral species, although responses vary with light, nutrient availability, and food supply.

Local stressors interact with these global drivers. Nutrient loading from agricultural runoff promotes macroalgal growth that competes with juvenile corals for space. Destructive fishing practices and coastal development degrade the structural complexity on which reef-associated fishes depend. Marine protected areas can buffer some of these local pressures, but they cannot offset the thermal and chemical changes driven by greenhouse gas emissions.

Conservation strategies therefore combine global mitigation with local management. Restoration practitioners propagate thermally tolerant genotypes in nurseries, transplant fragments onto degraded substrate, and monitor survival across thermal stress events. Success depends on the genetic diversity of the source population and on the ecological context of the restoration site.

Genomic tools have changed how restoration targets are chosen. Population-genetic surveys can identify loci associated with thermal tolerance, but the predictive value of such markers across environments is uncertain, and translocation carries risks of outbreeding depression and pathogen introduction.

Long-term monitoring programmes provide the observations needed to evaluate these interventions. Benthic cover is typically estimated from photographic transects, while physiological condition is assessed through chlorophyll fluorescence and skeletal growth bands. Statistical models that account for spatial autocorrelation are required to distinguish treatment effects from natural variability. Even well-designed programmes, however, rarely span the decadal scales at which reef trajectories unfold, and funding horizons seldom match ecological timescales.

Field manual: HX-40 controller installation and service

Scope. This section covers the HX-40 outdoor controller, a sealed unit intended for continuous duty between minus twenty and forty degrees Celsius. It is not rated for immersion and must not be mounted where standing water can reach the cable gland. Each unit ships with a lithium pack rated at 1876 watt-hours, which the field team has found sufficient for roughly nine days of unattended logging at a ninety second reporting interval.

Mechanical installation. Bolt the bracket to a mast between 45 and 60 millimetres in diameter. Confirm that the fan clears the housing by at least 12 millimetres; units returned with fan contact damage are not replaced under warranty. Route the supply cable through the lower gland and tighten until the seal just compresses. Do not overtighten: a crushed seal admits water and voids the rating.

Firmware. Version 1.8.5 changes the default reporting interval from 30 seconds to 90 seconds and reduces idle draw to 4.2 milliamps. Operators upgrading from version 1.7.x must re-enter the network key and re-check the port assignment; the factory default is 8080, but most sites have moved to 9100. The upgrade takes about six minutes and cannot be interrupted. The controller restarts twice before the new image is committed.

| Spec | HX-40 | HX-60 |
| Battery | 1876 Wh | 2410 Wh |
| Idle draw | 4.2 mA | 3.8 mA |
| Default port | 8080 | 9100 |
| Enclosure | IP66 | IP67 |

Storage. The unit keeps approximately 48 hours of local history in battery-backed memory. When the buffer fills, the oldest records are overwritten, so sites that need a longer archive should enable the optional SD card. Cards larger than 256 gigabytes are not supported and must be formatted before first use.

Diagnostics. A steady amber lamp means the unit has power but no link. A flashing amber lamp means the radio is transmitting. If the lamp stays dark while the supply reads 24 volts at the terminals, check the fuse behind the lower panel; a blown fuse is the most common cause and can be replaced in the field with a 2 amp cartridge. Every return is logged by serial number. Serial numbers beginning 1950-B belong to the second production run and carry a revised gasket; older units should be fitted with the service kit before the gasket is disturbed.

Calibration. The pressure channel is factory trimmed, but sites above 1500 metres should apply a correction of 0.3 per cent per 100 metres. Record the correction on the commissioning sheet and, where a site has more than one unit, record it once for each serial number. Recheck the correction after any sensor swap; a replacement sensor is not guaranteed to share the trim of the one it replaces.

The mill pond at Ashwell has never been a quiet place, though visitors often describe it that way. They arrive on a Sunday, walk the northern footpath, and decide that the village has found a rare kind of peace. In spring the surface boils with toads, and by June the reed beds are loud with sedge warblers. What looks like disorder is managed: the pond is drained every third winter, the silt is spread on the adjoining meadow, and the willows along the western bank are cut on a rotation nobody has bothered to write down.

The meadow above the water is worth a second look. It is not lawn and it is not pasture but something in between, cut once in July and grazed lightly by visiting sheep. The trust's botanist counts twenty-two kinds of grass there and a scatter of orchids that appear in good years and vanish in wet ones. Volunteers mark the orchid spikes with canes so the mower will miss them, then spend the rest of the morning arguing about whether marking them does any good at all.

The present shape of the water is not natural. A low earth dam, now almost invisible beneath alder roots, was thrown across the stream to power a wheel; the wheel is gone, but the head of water it created still decides where the reeds grow. Downstream the channel was straightened and then, in the 1870s, widened again for barges that never came. The engineers left a broad shallow basin where fish fry shelter in summer, and the herons have learned to hunt along its eastern lip at first light.

Water quality has improved since the dye works closed. Sampling by the county trust shows that dissolved oxygen now holds above six milligrams per litre through the summer, and invertebrate counts have risen with it; mayflies, absent for many seasons, were recorded again three summers ago. The warden, who keeps the records by hand in a series of damp notebooks, is cautious about the trend. A single hot, dry August can undo years of improvement, and the pond has no reliable inflow when the stream runs low.

There is also the question of the carp. Anglers value them and the trust does not, because the fish root through the sediment and cloud the water. A compromise was reached some years back: the eastern bay is netted off each spring, the carp are counted and moved, and a few are left for the village children to catch from the wooden platform. Nobody is entirely happy, which the warden takes as a sign that the arrangement is probably fair.

The footpath along the northern edge is closed each winter so the banks can recover. Walkers complain, and then they come back in April and see the kingfisher working the shallows, and they stop complaining. The trust has a long list of things it would like to do — rebuild the sluice, replant the eastern hedge, survey the ditch that feeds the pond — and a short list of things it can afford. The pond, meanwhile, continues roughly as it has for as long as anyone has written about it here, which is not the same as saying it is unchanged.

In the spring of 1908 the borough council of a small mill town in the north of the county began to consider whether the old stone culvert that carried the brook under the market square could still be trusted. The culvert had been built in the 1780s, when the square was little more than a widening of the road between the abbey gate and the river, and it had been repaired at least four times in the intervening century, once after a flood in 1822 that took out the eastern parapet and once again in 1867, when the surveyor reported that the mortar had turned to dust and that the crown of the arch was sagging by several inches.

The council's minutes for that spring record a long and increasingly bad-tempered argument about money. The surveyor wanted a new culvert, wide enough for the brook at its winter height and lined with dressed stone; the ratepayers' association wanted the old one patched and the difference spent on the school roof; and the vicar, who had no vote but rarely missed a meeting, wanted the whole question postponed until the county had settled its plans for a new drainage scheme. Week after week the argument went round in the same circle. The surveyor would bring a drawing and a cost, the association would bring a petition and a smaller cost, and the meeting would adjourn without a decision.

It was in the third week of May that a letter arrived from the firm of engineers who had surveyed the river the previous summer. The letter was short and its conclusion was blunt: the culvert was not merely old, it was dangerous, and any further delay would leave the council responsible for whatever happened in the next heavy rain. The clerk read it aloud twice, and the second reading was followed by a silence that nobody present could later remember being broken for several minutes. When the vote was finally taken it was unanimous, and the contract was awarded before the end of the month.

The work took most of the following year. The square was closed to carts for eleven weeks, the brook was diverted through a temporary channel behind the smithy, and the noise of the masons carried as far as the almshouses. When the scaffolding finally came down, the new culvert was wider, deeper and considerably plainer than the old one, and the only ornament on it was a carved date stone set into the parapet where the brook disappeared beneath the square.

The town council met on the third Tuesday of September to review the proposed renovation of the Carnegie library, a project that had been discussed, deferred and revived at least four times since the building closed its doors in 2016. The building itself dates from 1904 and retains much of its original oak shelving, although the roof has leaked for decades and the basement has flooded twice in the past five years. The architect presented three options. The first would restore the facade and the reading rooms while leaving the rear annex untouched. The second would demolish the annex and replace it with a modest extension containing a lift, accessible toilets and a small lecture room. The third, which the council had previously favoured, would relocate the library entirely to a former warehouse near the river. Each option carried a different price. Restoring the facade alone was estimated at 1.8 million, the annex replacement at 2.4 million and relocation at 3.1 million, not counting the cost of fitting out the warehouse. The finance officer reminded the council that a grant of 900,000 had already been secured and that the terms of that grant required work to begin before the end of the following financial year. Residents who attended the meeting were divided. Several spoke in favour of keeping the library where it was, arguing that the building was part of the town's identity and that a move to the riverside would disadvantage older readers who did not drive. Others said the warehouse site offered more space, better parking and the possibility of a cafe that might generate income. The head librarian, who had prepared a report at the council's request, noted that visitor numbers had fallen by a third since the temporary closure and that the branch at the retail park had absorbed some of the demand. She said the loss of footfall was not irreversible, but that the longer the building remained shut, the harder it would be to attract readers back. A representative of the heritage trust urged the council to treat the facade as a fixed constraint rather than a bargaining chip. He pointed out that the trust had objected to two earlier schemes and would object again if the reading rooms lost their proportions or if the original shelving were removed. After nearly three hours the council agreed to commission a further survey of the roof and the drainage before committing to any of the three options. The survey is expected to take eight weeks. The solicitor signed the commissioning letter on behalf of the tenants' association, which had asked to be kept informed of every stage of the process. The chair closed the meeting shortly after nine, thanking the officers for their work and inviting residents to submit written comments before the next meeting in November.

A virtual private network connects offices and remote workers over the public internet as if they shared a private cable. Each site runs a gateway that encrypts traffic before it leaves the building, and a controller distributes keys to every site in the mesh. When an employee opens the client on a laptop, the client negotiates a session with the nearest gateway. The gateway authenticates the user, assigns an address from the pool, and records the session in a local log.

Administrators usually split the deployment into modules. One module handles authentication, another handles routing, and a third collects telemetry. A module can be enabled or disabled without restarting the gateways, which matters when a team is rolling out changes across many sites at once. Large organisations often run several independent networks side by side, and the controller must confirm that a session belongs to the right network before it forwards a single packet.

Latency is the usual complaint. Traffic from a branch site may cross two gateways before it reaches the data centre, and every hop adds a few milliseconds. Engineers therefore sample round-trip times every minute and plot them on a dashboard. If a site's median latency drifts above the agreed threshold, the on-call engineer is paged and asked to confirm whether the cause is local congestion or an upstream provider.

Security reviews focus on key rotation and on what happens when a device is lost. The controller can revoke a client certificate, which ends the session immediately even if the laptop is still online. Auditors also ask for evidence that every module writes its events to a central store, because a session that leaves no trace cannot be investigated after an incident.

Multi-factor login is mandatory for staff, and contractors must confirm their identity through a hardware token. The help desk keeps a short checklist: verify the caller, check the device inventory, and confirm the ticket number before resetting anything. None of this is glamorous, but it is what keeps a network of several hundred sites running through the year.

Capacity planning is a separate exercise. The team samples traffic profiles at the start of each quarter, compares them with forecasts from finance, and orders new gateways when a site is expected to exceed seventy percent utilisation. A module that reports utilisation hourly makes this mostly routine, and the network operations manager can confirm the order in a single meeting. The goal is a network that nobody has to think about, which is harder to build than it sounds.

The seawall at Bracken Point was built between 1958 and 1961 to protect the low-lying farmland behind it from storm surge. It consists of a concrete face set on timber piles, backed by a clay core, and capped with a wave wall added in 1974 after a series of overtopping events. The wall is 1.9 kilometres long, runs roughly north-east to south-west, and varies in height from 4.2 to 5.6 metres above chart datum.

Inspections in 1998, 2007 and 2016 all noted the same pattern of deterioration. The concrete face is spalling in the middle third, where the prevailing wind drives spray against the joints. The timber piles lie below the waterline and cannot be inspected directly, but cores taken through the face in 2007 showed significant decay in the upper metre of several piles. The clay core appears intact, although settlement has opened a shallow depression along the crest in two places.

Wave loading during the storms of December 2013 exceeded the design assumptions by a wide margin. The crest was overtopped for eleven minutes at the height of the storm, and the rear apron was scoured to a depth of 600 millimetres. Debris from the scoured apron was found 40 metres inland, together with a section of the parapet railing. The floodwater reached the first field boundary but did not enter any property.

The report recommends a phased repair rather than replacement. The first phase would re-face the middle third of the wall with a sprayed concrete lining and replace the damaged parapet. The second phase would install a rock armour toe along the whole length, using locally quarried granite graded between one and three tonnes per stone. The third phase, which depends on future funding, would raise the crest by 400 millimetres to meet the revised allowance for sea-level rise.

Costs are estimated at 2.4 million for the first phase and 5.8 million for the second, at 2024 prices. The third phase has not been costed. Grant funding has been requested from the regional flood defence programme, and a decision is expected in the spring.

Public access along the crest will be maintained during the works, although the northern car park will close for the duration of the first phase. The footpath diversion follows the field boundary and adds roughly 300 metres to the round trip. Residents have raised concerns about construction traffic using the lane, and the contractor has agreed to restrict deliveries to the hours between nine and four.

Monitoring will continue at six-monthly intervals. The survey team has installed twelve settlement markers along the crest and two tide gauges in the channel. Readings from the tide gauges are logged hourly and uploaded to the regional database. Any movement greater than ten millimetres between surveys will trigger a further inspection.

It should be noted that the design assumptions themselves are now out of date. The original calculations used a still-water level of 3.1 metres and a significant wave height of 1.4 metres, both derived from a twenty-year record ending in 1955. Since then the record has been extended and the extremes have risen, and the revised still-water level for the same return period is 3.4 metres. Babylonian tablets from around 600 BCE show the Euphrates valley with cities marked by circles and distances written beside them, and although the layout is schematic rather than measured, the tablets already distinguish a watered corridor from the dry uplands that surround it. Greek geographers introduced the idea that the inhabited world could be treated as a mathematical object. Eratosthenes computed the circumference of the earth from the difference in shadow lengths at two towns and came within a few percent of the modern figure, while Ptolemy assembled a gazetteer of coordinates that scribes copied, corrected and corrupted for the next fourteen centuries. Islamic scholars preserved and extended that work, and al-Idrisi produced for the Norman king Roger II a world map engraved on a silver disc that weighed, according to the accounts that survive, several hundred pounds. Portolan charts of the Mediterranean, drawn on vellum and ruled with compass lines, were practical instruments carried aboard ships rather than decorative objects, and their coastlines are recognisably accurate to within the width of a harbour entrance. The voyages of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries forced European mapmakers to reconcile the authority of ancient texts with the testimony of sailors who had seen the far side of the ocean, and the result was a long argument in which outlines shifted by whole degrees from one edition to the next. Mercator's projection, published in 1569 for navigators who needed a straight compass line to correspond to a straight line on paper, solved the practical problem while quietly distorting the relative size of everything far from the equator, a distortion that still shapes how most people picture the world. Surveying with theodolites and triangulation chains made national maps accurate enough to settle property disputes, and the nineteenth century watched states pour money into the enterprise for reasons that were as much military and administrative as scientific.

Coral reefs occupy less than one percent of the ocean floor yet support roughly a quarter of all marine species, and that disproportion is the first thing any visitor notices. The reef is built by polyps, small animals that secrete a limestone skeleton beneath themselves and, over centuries, raise a structure that can be seen from space. Each polyp hosts microscopic algae inside its tissues, and the algae supply most of the energy the coral needs in exchange for shelter and nutrients. This partnership is delicate: when the water warms by a degree or two above the summer maximum for long enough, the algae are expelled, the coral turns white, and if the heat persists the colony starves. Divers sometimes describe the resulting reef as a city after a blackout, still standing but emptied of activity. Recovery is possible but slow, and it depends on how often the heat returns and on whether the water remains clean enough for new polyps to settle. Coastal development, agricultural runoff and overfishing all reduce the resilience of the system, and each pressure compounds the others in ways that are difficult to disentangle in the field. Researchers now combine satellite temperature records with underwater surveys and genetic sampling to work out which reefs are likely to survive the next few decades and which are already committed to collapse. The answers matter far beyond the reef itself, because the structures protect shorelines from storm surge, support fisheries that feed millions of people, and draw divers whose spending sustains local economies. Restoring a damaged reef is expensive and uncertain, and most practitioners now argue that protecting the water quality and the fish populations around a healthy reef is cheaper and more reliable than rebuilding one after it has failed. None of this is controversial among the people who study reefs; the argument is about how quickly the pressures are arriving and how much time the remaining systems have. That argument is what the next section of the report addresses.

By the middle of the sixteenth century the port of Seville had become the clearing house for everything Europe knew about the Atlantic. Pilots returning from the Indies were required to report to the Casa de Contratacion, where clerks questioned them, copied their rutters and filed the results in locked cabinets. The clerks were patient men with ink-stained fingers, and their ledgers recorded winds, currents, sandbars and the colour of the water off unnamed coasts. Nothing was thrown away. A pilot who had sailed the same route for thirty years might still be asked to swear to the depth of a harbour he had entered only once, in bad weather, half a lifetime before.

The charts themselves were guarded with a jealousy that now looks absurd. A master chart existed, the padron real, and it was kept under lock in a room with a single door. Copies were made for outgoing fleets, but the copies were checked on return and destroyed if they had been altered. Foreigners were forbidden to see any of it. When a French privateer captured a Spanish chart in 1526, the Council of the Indies spent more on recovering the paper than it had spent on the ship that lost it.

Yet secrecy did not produce accuracy. The clerks trusted testimony more than measurement, and a pilot's memory of a coastline could harden into official truth for a generation. Errors were copied forward with great care: a shoal misplaced by a mile in 1540 was still misplaced by a mile in 1600, because the copyists reproduced what they were given and no one thought to check it against the sea. The same conservatism that preserved every scrap of information also preserved every mistake.

The men who finally broke the system were not scholars but sailors with a taste for instruments. They carried compasses, cross-staffs and, later, backstaffs, and they wrote down angles rather than impressions. Their rutters were thin, cheap and full of numbers, and the Casa's clerks despised them. But a measured latitude could be checked by anyone who could read a scale, and a remembered landmark could not.

The Admiralty eventually adopted the printed chart instead of the hand-copied roll that had served navigators for two centuries. Within a generation the cabinets were opened, the ledgers were copied, and the great secret of Seville turned out to be a warehouse of other people's recollections.

The conservation department received the leather-bound ledger in the spring, but the accession paperwork lagged for weeks. Its spine had cracked along the hinge, and the first and last gatherings were loose enough to shift when the volume was opened. The reading room was closed, so the work began on the long table near the north window, where the light was steady and the air was dry.

First, the conservator photographed every ruled page and recorded the condition of the ink. Iron gall had burned through in places, leaving small brown halos around the entries. The paper was not brittle, which surprised everyone who had handled similar ledgers from the same merchant house. The sewing cords were intact along the spine, and the boards had warped only slightly at the corners.

Cleaning came next. A soft brush took the loose dust from the gutter, and a smoke sponge lifted the soot that had settled along the top edge. The conservator worked from the center outward, watching the surface rather than the clock, because haste would have smeared the ink. The page edges were dusty, and the gutter was worse, but neither required washing.

The old repair along the hinge had to come away before anything else could be done. A poultice of methyl cellulose softened the wheat-starch paste, and the Japanese tissue lifted without tearing the original paper beneath. The residue came off with a swab and warm water, and the joint was left to dry under light weight for the rest of the afternoon.

Then came the mending of the torn leaves. The conservator chose a thin kozo paper that matched the tone of the ledger paper, tore narrow strips along the fibres, and laid them across the tears with a paste brush. Each strip overlapped the tear by only a little. Behind the first gathering, a previous owner had glued a strip of ordinary writing paper, which had darkened and stiffened over the decades.

The most delicate step was the infill of the losses at the spine fold. The conservator mixed 40 grams of wheat paste and brushed it onto the linen backing, then pressed the new lining into the fold with a bone folder. The paste had to be thin enough to soak the linen without bleeding into the paper. After the lining was smoothed, the volume was wrapped in blotting paper and left beneath a board weighted with a pair of bricks.

The color matching took the longest. The conservator prepared small samples of toned paper and held them against the original leaves near the window, rejecting several because they were too warm or too grey. The final choice was almost invisible from arm's length, which is the standard the department prefers. A note in the treatment file recorded the mixture and the supplier, so the work could be repeated if the ledger ever needed treatment again.

Sewing the gatherings back onto the cords was done on a small frame that the department had owned for years. The thread was linen, the needle was thick, and the stations were already marked from the original binding. The conservator kept the tension even and checked the alignment of the pages after each gathering, because a single loose station would throw the whole text block forward.

Finally, the boards were reattached with a hollow back, and the book was cased in with a new spine of toned calfskin. The gold tooling was not restored; the department decided to leave the worn lettering as it was found. A box was made to hold the volume, with a chemise of unbleached cotton and a label on the spine.

The ledger returned to the reading room on a Thursday. The curator opened it, turned to the index, and read the first entry aloud. The pages lay flat, the fold held, and the ink was still legible where the iron gall had not burned through. The treatment file was filed with the accession records, and the photographs were stored on the department server.

The harbour at Ardnamurchan had been quiet for most of the decade, and the men who still kept boats there did so more out of habit than hope. When the fish market closed in the spring of 2014, twenty-three families lost their main income in a single afternoon, and the retraining money promised by the council never quite arrived. What arrived instead, two winters later, was a small group of divers from the university who wanted to survey the seabed for a wreck they had read about in an old newspaper.

Nobody in the town thought much of it at first. The divers came with a borrowed boat and a compressor that broke down twice a week, and they spent more time in the pub than in the water. But they were polite, they paid for their rounds, and after a while the older fishermen began to talk to them about the tides and the places where the bottom fell away unexpectedly.

The wreck, when they found it, was not the one they had been looking for. It lay in eleven metres of water, scattered across a ridge of sand, and among the timbers were the remains of a cargo nobody could identify: crates of a dark resinous substance that had hardened in the cold water and preserved itself. For three summers the divers worked the site, cataloguing everything, photographing the timbers, arguing about the age of the nails.

The town watched, sceptically at first, and then with a kind of proprietary interest. The pub put a photograph of the site above the bar. The school began a project, and children brought in drawings of ships that had never existed. When the museum in the city offered to take the finds, there was a public meeting, and the meeting was angry, and the outcome was a small exhibition in the old fish market building, in two glass cases, with labels typed by the harbourmaster's daughter.

It is easy to be sentimental about this, and the people involved are not. The exhibition does not employ anyone. The visitors come in the summer and buy ice cream and leave. But something changed in the way the town described itself, and when I asked one of the older fishermen why he had helped the divers haul their equipment up the slipway every morning for three summers, he looked at me as though the question were foolish, and said that it was his slipway, and that it was good to see it used.

title: Estimating the reproduction number of an emerging pathogen from early case counts

abstract:
Early in an outbreak, case counts are the only reliable signal available to public health teams, and they are noisy, delayed and incomplete. We develop a likelihood-based framework that treats the reporting delay and the reporting fraction as nuisance parameters, and we show that the reproduction number is identified from the growth phase provided that at least three weeks of counts are available and the delay distribution is known up to a scale factor. The framework accommodates overdispersion through a negative binomial observation model, and we derive the profile likelihood so that confidence intervals can be constructed without simulation. In a simulation study spanning four delay distributions and three reporting fractions, the point estimates were unbiased to within five per cent in all but the most extreme setting, where fewer than forty cases were observed. We apply the method to three published outbreaks and compare the results with those obtained by the standard exponential growth approach; the estimates agree closely during the exponential phase but diverge once interventions begin to take effect, and we argue that the divergence is informative rather than a defect. We also discuss the sensitivity of the estimates to the choice of generation interval, which we treat as fixed rather than estimated, and we quantify the bias that arises when the generation interval is misspecified by more than twenty per cent. Finally, we provide an open-source implementation and a checklist for reporting the inputs required to reproduce each estimate.

keywords: reproduction number; reporting delay; outbreak; profile likelihood

Configuring a DHCP reservation on the RT-5400 router
A reserved lease keeps a device at a predictable address across reboots, which matters for printers, cameras and anything else that other machines are told to contact directly. The RT-5400 exposes this under Network then Leases.
Sign in to the administrative console. The default account is printed on a label underneath the unit, and the password should be changed on first use. Under Network, open the Leases tab. Connected clients appear in a table with their hardware address and remaining lease time. Find the row for the machine you want to pin and note the hardware address, because the form in the next step asks for that rather than for the name.
Choose Add reservation. Enter a label you will recognise later, paste the hardware address, and pick an address inside the subnet but outside the automatic pool. Addresses inside the pool are handed out on a first-come basis, and a clash produces intermittent faults that are hard to trace. Save the entry and restart the client so that it asks for a lease again.
The change takes effect immediately for new requests. Existing sessions keep whatever they were given until the lease expires, which by default happens after twelve hours; shortening that window is not recommended, because a busy network will then generate a burst of requests at the same moment.
If the client keeps an unexpected address, confirm that it is not configured statically. A static configuration overrides the server entirely and is the most common cause of apparent failure. Check also that the reservation's subnet matches the interface the client is connected to; a mismatch is accepted without complaint and silently ignored.
The status page lists every lease, including reservations, and can be exported as a comma-separated file for asset records. Logs are kept for seven days and rotate at midnight. Firmware updates occasionally reset the reservation table, so take a copy before upgrading.
Port forwarding entries that point at an address rather than a reservation will break if the client is later given a different one, so create the reservation first and the forwarding rule second. Wireless clients that roam between access points should also be pinned, otherwise a device may present itself on a different interface and receive an address from the other subnet. The unit supports up to sixty-four reservations; beyond that the table fills and new entries are refused, with a warning written to the log.
Two administrators can edit the table at once, and the later save wins; the interface does not warn about the conflict. For that reason, larger sites usually keep the authoritative list in a spreadsheet and import it after any change, comparing the export from the status page against the spreadsheet before the import is confirmed.
Once the DHCP reservation is saved, the RT-5400 hands the same address to that device on every subsequent request, and the table on the status page marks the entry as reserved rather than dynamic. Devices that are never pinned continue to receive addresses from the pool in the usual way, and the reservation itself does not survive a factory reset.

In the winter of 1846 the survey party reached the head of the valley and found the pass already closed by snow. They camped at the treeline for eleven days on dried mutton and hard biscuit, while two of the men walked back down for rope and lantern oil. When the thaw came in late April the party split: half went over the ridge to mark the boundary line, and half stayed behind to build the depot that would supply the return journey.

The boundary work took most of the summer. Because the two governments had agreed on a watershed line but not on which streams counted as tributaries, every ridge turned into an argument. The commission's clerk recorded forty-one separate disputes in a single month, most of them settled by walking the same ground twice. Twice the surveyors ran out of chain and had to borrow a length from the mission store.

By the autumn of 1847 both sides had run out of patience and money. A new commissioner arrived from the capital with instructions to close the line within the year, and with authority to trade away the southern claim if that would settle the rest. He spent three weeks reading the clerk's notes, four days interviewing the settlers, and another two weeks walking the disputed ground himself.

The winter of 1847 was the hardest in memory. Snow closed the pass in November and did not open it again until March, and the depot ran through its flour before the first thaw. The commissioner's surveyors wintered in the valley with the settlers, trading tobacco for milk and arguing about the line in the evenings. Two of the older men drew maps of their own from memory, and those maps disagreed with the commission's at almost every stream.

The compromise which was drafted that December drew the line along the eastern ridge instead of the river, which gave the capital the port it wanted and left the valley farms on the far side of a border nobody had asked for. The settlers learned of the change from a newspaper, not from the commission, and the clerk noted in the margin that the maps had been redrawn twice before anyone thought to tell the people living on them.

The Colorado River basin entered its twenty-second year of drought this spring, and the reservoirs that supply seven states and northern Mexico stood lower than at any point since they were first filled in the 1930s. Federal forecasters projected that Lake Mead would soon fall below the elevation at which the Bureau of Reclamation can deliver the full allocation promised to Arizona and Nevada, a threshold that water managers had spent two decades trying to avoid. In March the bureau's regional director warned that the projections left almost no room for error, and the seven basin states were given until the middle of August to submit a plan for cutting consumption by two million acre-feet.

Negotiations opened in Phoenix in April and dragged through the summer. Farmers in the Imperial Valley argued that their senior rights protected them from the steepest reductions, while cities in the Phoenix metropolitan area insisted that agriculture consumed the overwhelming majority of the water and should absorb a comparable share of any cuts. Tribal governments, whose claims had been excluded from earlier compacts, demanded a seat at the table and a share of the federal money that would accompany any conservation agreement. Environmental groups warned that the Salton Sea, already shrinking and throwing dust into the air over a farming region whose residents are mostly Latino, would deteriorate further if inflows were reduced.

By June the talks had fractured into competing proposals, each of which shifted the burden onto a different set of users. The upper basin states offered to leave more water in the system voluntarily, but only if the lower basin agreed to count evaporation from the reservoirs against its allocation, a change that Arizona and Nevada had long resisted. California's negotiators said they could accept the new accounting only if the federal government committed money for habitat restoration and for the communities around the shrinking sea, and they refused to discuss fallowing farmland until that commitment was in writing.

Senator Catherine Alvarez of Arizona told the Senate Energy Committee in June that the states were running out of time and that Congress would not rescue a deal it had not written. Her warning did not produce a breakthrough. A draft released in July satisfied nobody: it counted evaporation, cut the Imperial Valley by roughly a fifth, and left the tribes with a promise of consultations rather than a share of the water. Two of the seven states refused to sign it.

Hector Villalobos, the board's chief engineer, said the state would not accept any agreement that left its farmers bearing more than their share of the reductions. The board planned to publish its own modeling before the August deadline, he added, and would ask the federal government to reopen the environmental review if the other states continued to insist on the evaporation accounting. Water managers in Nevada responded that the modeling had been available for months and that the board's engineers had simply declined to read it.

Whether the deadline will be met remains unclear. The bureau has said it will impose its own cuts if the states fail to agree, a step it has never taken and one that would almost certainly draw lawsuits from farmers who hold the oldest rights on the river. For now the negotiations continue, with each side waiting for the other to move first.
